title: Rehabilitacija riparijalnih zelenih koridora uklanjanjem Amorpha fruticosa: trogodišnji monitoring autohtonih vrsta
abstract: Prikazani su rezultati trogodišnjeg monitoringa (2020–2022) na 10 lokaliteta duž kanala Begej i DTD, gde su 2019. godine sprovedene mere mehaničkog uklanjanja Amorpha fruticosa u kombinaciji sa sadnjom autohtonih žbunova (Cornus sanguinea, Sambucus nigra, Viburnum opulus). Kontrolne parcele su ostavljene bez intervencije. Na tretiranim parcelama praćeni su preživljavanje sadnica, pokrivenost autohtonih vrsta, rekolonizacija A. fruticosa i diverzitet herbasnog sloja. Nakon tri godine, preživljavanje sadnica kretalo se od 61% (V. opulus) do 79% (C. sanguinea). Pokrivenost autohtonih žbunova u tretiranim parcelama bila je statistički značajno veća nego u kontrolama (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.01). Rekolonizacija A. fruticosa bila je primetan problem na 7 od 10 lokaliteta, što ukazuje na neophodnost višegodišnjeg naknadnog održavanja. Rad daje konkretne preporuke za protokole restauracije.

title: Enforceability of Sukuk Covenants under Slovenian and Serbian Civil Law: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: This paper examines whether the contractual architecture of sukuk—specifically asset-transfer clauses and profit-distribution mechanisms—can be rendered enforceable under the civil-law frameworks of Slovenia and Serbia without statutory amendment. Using a doctrinal method, the study analyses forty-three sukuk prospectuses issued between 2004 and 2009 and maps each structural element to existing contract and property law provisions in both jurisdictions. Findings indicate that asset-backed sukuk structures face the most significant obstacles in Serbian law due to restrictions on beneficial ownership, while Slovenian fiduciary transfer provisions offer a partial functional equivalent. The paper identifies three legislative lacunae in each jurisdiction and proposes minimal textual amendments to existing civil codes that would accommodate sukuk issuance without creating a parallel regulatory regime. The study contributes to the emerging literature on Islamic finance transplantation into non-common-law environments and is among the first to address the Serbian context specifically.

title: Murabaha as a Lending Substitute: Regulatory Treatment under the EU Consumer Credit Directive
abstract: Murabaha—a cost-plus-profit sale used as an alternative to interest-bearing loans—is increasingly marketed to Muslim retail clients in EU member states. This paper investigates whether murabaha products offered by institutions in Austria, Germany, and the United Kingdom prior to Brexit satisfy the disclosure, APR-calculation, and cooling-off requirements of Directive 2008/48/EC. The analysis draws on product documentation collected from eight financial institutions and two legal opinions issued by national regulators. The study finds that standard murabaha documentation systematically fails to express the profit margin as an annual percentage rate, creating compliance risk under the Directive. It further argues that the Directive's definition of 'total cost of credit' is broad enough to capture murabaha profit without amendment, provided national supervisors issue interpretive guidance. Three supervisory approaches adopted in the UK, Luxembourg, and Ireland are benchmarked as regulatory templates for continental jurisdictions.

title: Capital Treatment of Ijara Contracts under Basel III: Lease or Loan?
abstract: Ijara, an Islamic leasing instrument, presents classification difficulties for prudential supervisors because it shares economic characteristics with both operating leases and secured lending. This paper analyses how ijara should be treated under the Basel III capital adequacy framework, with particular focus on risk-weighted asset computation and the leverage ratio. Using a sample of sixteen ijara agreements from Gulf Cooperation Council institutions operating in European markets, the paper applies the Basel Committee's criteria for on- and off-balance-sheet treatment and compares results with accounting classifications under IFRS 16. The study finds that identical ijara structures receive divergent capital charges depending on national supervisor interpretation, producing competitive distortions between Islamic and conventional banks. A proposed classification decision tree is developed and tested against the sample agreements. The paper also discusses the relevance of the EBA's 2016 discussion paper on proportionality in regulatory treatment of alternative finance products.

title: Islamic Finance in the Western Balkans: Demand-Side Survey Evidence from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, and North Macedonia
abstract: This study reports findings from a structured questionnaire survey of 1,240 adult respondents in three Western Balkan states, conducted in 2013, examining awareness of and stated preferences for Islamic financial products. The survey instrument covered savings accounts, home-purchase financing, and small-business lending. Results indicate that awareness of Islamic finance products is highest in Bosnia and Herzegovina (62% of Muslim respondents), moderate in North Macedonia (38%), and low in Serbia (19%), while stated willingness to use such products if available exceeds awareness in all three markets, suggesting latent demand. Multivariate logistic regression identifies age, religiosity index, and prior banking experience as significant predictors of stated preference. The paper discusses regulatory preconditions for market entry and estimates minimum viable market size for a standalone Islamic retail banking unit in each jurisdiction, drawing on population data and deposit statistics from national central banks.

title: Shariah Supervisory Boards and Corporate Governance: Accountability Gaps in European Subsidiaries of Islamic Banks
abstract: Islamic financial institutions operating in Europe typically maintain shariah supervisory boards (SSBs) to certify product compliance, yet European company law provides no statutory recognition of such bodies. This paper examines the governance implications of SSBs in fourteen Islamic financial institutions that held banking licences in EU or EEA jurisdictions as of 2015. Document analysis of annual reports, articles of association, and regulatory submissions reveals that SSB mandates are legally subordinated to supervisory board instructions in all fourteen cases, creating a potential conflict between religious and prudential oversight. The paper considers whether SSB members can be held liable under EU Directive 2013/36/EU fitness-and-properness requirements and concludes that the current framework contains a regulatory gap. Three governance models from the UK, Luxembourg, and Malaysia are reviewed and adapted to fit the one-tier and two-tier board structures prevalent in continental Europe.

title: Regulatory Barriers to Islamic Finance in Central and Eastern Europe: A Policy Comparison
abstract: This book chapter surveys the legislative and regulatory landscape for Islamic finance in eight Central and Eastern European states: Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia, and Serbia. Drawing on interviews with fourteen central bank officials and regulators conducted in 2016–2017, alongside a structured review of banking laws, tax codes, and securities regulations, the chapter maps specific legal provisions that create obstacles for Islamic finance products. The analysis finds that double-taxation of asset transfers in murabaha and ijara transactions represents the most uniformly cited barrier across jurisdictions, followed by the absence of a legal concept of beneficial ownership. The chapter also identifies Hungary and Serbia as having made the most substantive preliminary enquiries into enabling legislation, and discusses the political economy of reform in each case. The chapter concludes with a standardised reform checklist for policymakers.

title: Musharaka Venture Financing and the EU Prospectus Regulation: A Structural Compatibility Assessment
abstract: Musharaka is a partnership-based financing structure in which profits and losses are shared according to a pre-agreed ratio, functioning as an approximate equivalent to equity co-investment. This paper assesses whether musharaka instruments issued to retail investors in the EU require a prospectus under Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, focusing on the transferability criterion and the definition of 'securities' under Article 2(a). The study analyses twelve musharaka instruments marketed in Germany, France, and the Netherlands between 2012 and 2018, classifying each according to the four-part transferability test derived from ESMA guidance. Results indicate that seven of the twelve instruments meet the transferability threshold and should have been accompanied by a prospectus; in five cases, issuers relied on crowdfunding exemptions that the paper argues were inapplicable. The paper proposes a disclosure template adapted from the Key Information Document format specified in the PRIIPs Regulation that would be suitable for retail musharaka offerings.

title: Zakat and Tax Deductibility: Lessons for Serbian Fiscal Law from Malaysian and UK Precedents
abstract: Zakat—a mandatory charitable contribution under Islamic law—creates a dual-payment burden for Muslim taxpayers in jurisdictions that do not recognise it as a tax-deductible expenditure. This paper examines the fiscal treatment of zakat in Serbian income and corporate tax law and compares it with the treatment in Malaysia (where zakat offsets income tax liability directly) and the United Kingdom (where zakat qualifies as a charitable donation for Gift Aid purposes). The study uses a hypothetical taxpayer model to calculate the effective tax burden difference across the three systems for individuals at three income levels and one corporate entity. It finds that Serbian taxpayers face a de facto additional tax burden of between 10% and 15% of total tax liability if they fulfil zakat obligations, compared to a zero additional burden in Malaysia. The paper argues that a modest amendment to the Serbian Law on Income Tax could resolve the asymmetry without creating broader fiscal risks.

title: Green Sukuk and EU Sustainable Finance Taxonomy: Alignment and Gaps
abstract: Green sukuk—sukuk whose proceeds are restricted to environmentally beneficial projects—have been issued in Malaysia, Indonesia, and several Gulf states since 2017. This paper examines whether the asset eligibility criteria and reporting requirements of green sukuk frameworks published by the Securities Commission Malaysia and the AAOIFI align with the technical screening criteria of the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852. The study compares eligibility criteria across six environmental objectives, applying the Do No Significant Harm and minimum social safeguard tests to a sample of seventeen green sukuk issued between 2017 and 2021. Results indicate partial alignment for climate change mitigation (approximately 70% of criteria matched) but significant gaps in biodiversity, water, and circular economy objectives. The paper also notes that the AAOIFI green sukuk standard lacks a forward-looking science-based target requirement, which is implicit in the EU Taxonomy's trajectory approach. Practical implications for European issuers seeking dual Islamic-and-green certification are discussed.

title: The Serbian National Bank's Prudential Framework and the Accommodation of Profit-and-Loss Sharing Deposits
abstract: Serbian banking regulation, based on the Law on Banks of 2005 as amended, defines deposits exclusively in terms of contractual interest obligations, leaving no explicit room for profit-and-loss sharing (PLS) deposit accounts, which are the retail funding instrument of Islamic banks. This paper analyses the statutory definition of 'deposit' and 'credit institution' under Serbian law and explores whether a domestic bank could offer PLS accounts under existing licence conditions or whether a dedicated licence category is required. The study interviews seven officials at the National Bank of Serbia (anonymised) and reviews regulatory correspondence obtained through freedom-of-information requests. The paper concludes that a PLS account with a guaranteed minimum principal—a common hybrid structure—would be legally classifiable as a deposit under current Serbian law, while a fully loss-bearing PLS account would not, and proposes a regulatory sandbox mechanism as an interim solution. Comparison is made with the Hungarian MNB's 2019 exploratory exercise.

title: Towards an Islamic Finance Window Regulation in Serbia: Drafting Principles and Comparative Benchmarks
abstract: A finance 'window' is a dedicated unit within a conventional bank licensed to offer shariah-compliant products, subject to ring-fencing requirements. This paper develops a set of drafting principles for a hypothetical Serbian Islamic finance window regulation, benchmarked against window frameworks in Turkey, Malaysia, Oman, and the United Kingdom. The study identifies eleven structural elements that any enabling regulation must address: licensing criteria, capital ring-fencing, shariah governance, product approval, liquidity management, deposit insurance, consumer protection, tax neutrality, resolution planning, supervisory reporting, and public disclosure. For each element, the paper compares the four benchmark jurisdictions, scores them on a six-point adequacy scale developed by the author, and derives a recommended approach for the Serbian context. The paper is intended as a direct input into ongoing consultations between the University of Novi Sad and the National Bank of Serbia on alternative finance.

title: AAOIFI vs. IFSB Standards: Practical Divergences for European Supervisors
abstract: The Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) and the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB) are the two principal international standard-setters for Islamic finance, but their standards overlap in scope and sometimes conflict in detail. This paper catalogues divergences between AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards and IFSB Prudential Standards as they apply to three instrument classes—sukuk, murabaha, and takaful—and assesses the practical implications for European national supervisors who must decide which standards to reference in domestic regulation or supervisory guidance. Using a structured comparison matrix applied to the most recent versions of relevant standards as of 2024, the paper identifies twenty-three material divergences, of which nine concern measurement or classification in ways that affect capital calculations. The paper also surveys how five European jurisdictions (Luxembourg, UK, France, Germany, Ireland) have referenced or ignored these standards in their existing guidance and identifies a pattern of selective borrowing that creates cross-border regulatory inconsistency.

title: Tacit Approval as a Facilitation Tool in Business Licensing: Lessons from Slovenia and Croatia for Serbia
abstract: Using semi-structured interviews with 23 senior civil servants and a review of licensing files across three economic sectors (food safety, construction, and environmental permits), this study assesses the practical effects of positive administrative silence regimes introduced in Slovenia in 2004 and Croatia in 2009. The research recorded outcomes in 380 licensing cases in each country over five years post-reform. Positive silence reduced average licensing time by 31 days in construction but had no statistically significant effect in environmental permitting, where third-party consultation requirements created exceptions. The study identifies implementation bottlenecks attributable to the absence of electronic dossier management and unclear rules on the documentary evidence required to trigger the silence clock. Recommendations are addressed specifically to the Serbian Ministry of Public Administration, which was consulting on a regulatory reform package at the time of writing.

title: The Right to Good Administration under Article 41 of the EU Charter and Its Horizontal Effects on Candidate State Administration
abstract: Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union codifies a right to have affairs handled impartially, fairly and within a reasonable time, but its direct applicability is confined to EU institutions and bodies. This chapter examines the extent to which the right to good administration nonetheless shapes administrative law reform in EU candidate states through the conditionality mechanism, case law of the Court of Justice, and the European Ombudsman's standards. The analysis draws on accession progress reports for Serbia, North Macedonia and Albania for the period 2014–2024 and codes 47 Commission recommendations relating to administrative procedure modernisation. The chapter argues that Article 41 functions as a soft constitutional template even where it lacks binding force, and that its influence on candidate state procedural reform is most visible in the area of time limits and the obligation to state reasons — with administrative silence representing a residual gap in transposition.

title: Teaching Administrative Law History in the Western Balkans: Curriculum Practices and Archival Resources
abstract: This short communication reports on a survey of administrative law curricula at 14 law faculties across six Western Balkan states, conducted in 2024, examining the extent to which the historical development of administrative jurisdiction is treated as a distinct subject or integrated into general administrative law courses. Responses from 29 faculty members show that historical content is present in all curricula but occupies fewer than 15 percent of contact hours in 11 of the 14 institutions surveyed. The paper also inventories available archival resources for teaching and research in the field, including digitised court registers from the Austrian State Archive, partially digitised files of the Yugoslav State Council held in Belgrade, and the as-yet undigitised administrative court records of the Banovinas held in regional archives in Novi Sad, Sarajevo, and Zagreb. The note proposes a minimum set of primary sources suitable for a regionally shared open-access teaching repository and calls for coordinated digitisation efforts.

title: Accuracy Assessment of GPR Depth Estimation for Buried PVC Water Pipes in Sandy Loam Soils
abstract: Ground-penetrating radar depth estimates for buried polyvinyl chloride water pipes depend strongly on the dielectric permittivity of the surrounding soil, which varies with moisture content and texture. This study presents controlled-trench experiments carried out at two test sites in Vojvodina, where 110 mm and 160 mm diameter PVC pipes were buried at known depths between 0.6 m and 1.8 m in sandy loam. A 400 MHz antenna was used with a GSSI SIR-3000 system. Permittivity was estimated by the common-midpoint method and cross-validated against time-domain reflectometry probes inserted at five depths per trench. Depth errors for the 400 MHz antenna ranged from 2.1% to 8.7%, with the largest errors occurring when volumetric water content exceeded 28%. A correction procedure based on a two-layer dielectric model reduced mean absolute depth error from 6.3 cm to 2.1 cm. Results indicate that routine moisture monitoring at GPR survey sites can substantially improve cadastral positioning accuracy for utility pipes.

title: A GIS Data Model for Urban Utility Cadastre Compliant with the Serbian Technical Regulation on Underground Installations
abstract: Serbia's technical regulation on underground installations, enacted in 2010, specifies minimum positional accuracy requirements and mandatory attribute sets for utility cadastres but provides no standardised data model. This paper proposes a relational GIS schema implemented in PostgreSQL with the PostGIS extension that maps regulation requirements to feature classes, topology rules and attribute domains. The schema covers six utility categories: water supply, sewerage, gas, district heating, electricity and telecommunications. Topology constraints enforce minimum pipe separation rules and flag intersections lacking documented crossing agreements. The model was populated with survey data for a 1.2 km² pilot area in Subotica municipality and validated against 1:500 municipal plans. Completeness ratio reached 94% for water and 71% for telecommunications, reflecting the poorer documentation state of the latter. The schema is published as an open-source QGIS plugin accompanying this paper.

title: Subsurface Utility Engineering for a 22 kV Underground Cable Replacement Project: Methodology and Lessons Learned
abstract: This book chapter describes the subsurface utility engineering process applied to a 3.4 km urban corridor in Zrenjanin, Serbia, where an ageing overhead 22 kV line was replaced by an underground cable. The chapter covers the full SUE quality level sequence from desk study through geophysical detection to test-hole verification. Desk-study sources included 1:2500 municipal cadastre sheets, utility operator records and historical aerial photographs from 1973 and 1988. GPR surveys with 250 MHz and 500 MHz antennas were conducted prior to open-cut construction; results were overlaid with cable route design drawings to identify conflict points. Seventeen previously unknown utility segments were discovered, triggering four route design revisions. The chapter discusses root causes of documentation gaps, including informal network extensions during the 1980s and post-war reconstruction, and proposes a project-phase checklist for Serbian distribution grid operators undertaking similar cable burial programmes.

title: Comparison of 3D GPR Migration Algorithms for Resolving Closely Spaced Parallel Pipes at Shallow Depth
abstract: When two pipes run in parallel at separation distances below the Rayleigh resolution limit of the antenna in use, standard B-scan interpretation underestimates pipe count and misestimates lateral positions. This study compared Kirchhoff migration, frequency-wavenumber migration and reverse-time migration applied to synthetic C-scan volumes and to field data collected over a test trench containing three 63 mm PE pipes at 0.7 m depth with 120 mm centre-to-centre spacing. The 900 MHz antenna was traversed in a 0.05 m × 0.05 m grid pattern over a 2 m × 2 m aperture. Kirchhoff migration separated the two outer pipes in 78% of synthetic realisations but failed to resolve the central pipe. Frequency-wavenumber migration resolved all three pipes in 91% of realisations and produced lateral position errors below 25 mm. Field validation using a reference frame showed mean lateral positioning error of 21 mm for frequency-wavenumber versus 54 mm for Kirchhoff. Processing time remained tractable on standard desktop hardware at under 90 seconds per C-scan volume.

title: Updating an Existing Utility Cadastre Using Mobile LiDAR and GPR: Workflow and Cost Analysis for a Peri-Urban Gas Distribution Area
abstract: Periodic cadastre updates are required when network extensions or repairs alter buried asset positions. This paper presents a workflow that couples a vehicle-mounted LiDAR scanner for above-ground reference frame acquisition with GPR for subsurface detection, tested on 18 km of peri-urban gas distribution network in Sremska Mitrovica, Serbia. LiDAR point clouds were georeferenced using GNSS/INS at 5 cm absolute accuracy and served as the spatial backbone onto which GPR detections were registered. Change detection between the updated cadastre and the prior 2011 record identified 64 newly installed segments, 11 relocated segments and 3 abandoned segments not recorded in any documentation. Cost comparison against a conventional resurvey using walking GPR and RTK-GNSS on the same corridor showed a 34% reduction in field time per kilometre, partially offset by higher data processing costs. The workflow is applicable to annual update cycles for medium-density distribution grids.

title: Quality Level Attribution of Existing Utility Records in Four Serbian Municipalities: A Systematic Audit
abstract: A reliable subsurface utility engineering programme requires knowing the quality level of existing records before planning intrusive works. This paper presents a systematic audit of utility documentation held by four Serbian municipalities covering a combined urban area of approximately 38 km². Records for water, sewerage, gas and electricity were evaluated against a four-tier quality framework adapted from the American CI/ASCE 38-02 standard and calibrated to Serbian regulatory requirements. Auditors reviewed 1,847 plan sheets and 423 digitised GIS layers, assessing completeness, positional accuracy, attribute richness and update frequency. Overall, 31% of reviewed records met quality level B or above; sewerage documentation was the weakest category, with 61% at quality level D. Municipalities with GIS-based cadastres introduced after 2010 performed significantly better than those retaining paper-only systems. The audit protocol is offered as a transferable tool for municipal geodetic services and utility operators preparing investment programmes.

title: GPR Signature Classification for Common Pipe Materials in Vojvodina Soils: A Laboratory and Field Study
abstract: Distinguishing pipe material from GPR reflections alone is commercially useful because material type determines corrosion risk and replacement priority. This laboratory and field study characterised GPR reflections from steel, cast iron, ductile iron, PVC and high-density polyethylene pipes of 63–315 mm diameter buried in reconstructed Vojvodina soil columns at 0.5–2.0 m depth. Four antenna frequencies (250, 500, 900 and 1600 MHz) were evaluated. Amplitude-versus-offset behaviour, reflection polarity and hyperbola apex sharpness were extracted as discriminating features and fed into a random forest classifier. In controlled conditions the classifier separated metallic from non-metallic pipes with 96% accuracy; distinguishing PVC from HDPE remained unreliable at all frequencies tested. Field trials over 12.1 km of surveyed distribution network in Ruma and Inđija showed that metallic versus non-metallic classification transferred to field conditions with 89% accuracy when soil moisture was below 20% volumetric content, degrading to 74% under wet conditions.

title: INSPIRE Compliance in Municipal Utility Cadastres: Mapping Serbian Practice to the Utility Networks Data Specification
abstract: The INSPIRE Directive's Utility Networks theme specifies a comprehensive data model for cross-border interoperability of network infrastructure data, but implementation among smaller European municipalities remains patchy. This paper examines the degree to which nine Serbian municipal utility cadastres produced between 2015 and 2024 conform to the INSPIRE Utility Networks Data Specification v3.0. Conformance was assessed across four dimensions: feature-type completeness, attribute population, coordinate reference system compliance, and metadata provision. Mean feature-type completeness was 58%; attribute population averaged 44% of mandatory attributes. Coordinate reference system compliance was universal, as EPSG:32634 is standard in Serbian cadastral practice. Metadata provision was the weakest dimension, with only two of nine cadastres supplying INSPIRE-compliant metadata records. A lightweight transformation toolkit implemented as a QGIS processing algorithm is described that maps the most common Serbian cadastre schemas to INSPIRE GML, reducing manual intervention required for cross-border data exchange.

title: Evaluating the fitness for purpose of the Serbian cadastral base map for use as a reference layer in municipal urban planning GIS
abstract: Municipal urban planning in Serbia relies on the cadastral base map as a primary spatial reference, yet no systematic assessment of its fitness for planning-specific purposes has been conducted at a national scale. This paper develops a fitness-for-purpose assessment framework based on six criteria—positional accuracy, completeness, topological correctness, attribute currency, semantic alignment with planning ontology, and access and licensing constraints—and applies it to the cadastral datasets of eight municipalities of varying size and development pressure in the Vojvodina and Šumadija regions. Data were obtained directly from municipal cadastral offices under a research agreement. Positional accuracy (assessed by GNSS check survey, n=2 400 points) varied from 0.3 m to 2.1 m RMSE across municipalities. Topological correctness was below 95% in six of eight municipalities. Attribute currency was rated adequate in three municipalities. The paper concludes with a scoring matrix and identifies the principal bottlenecks for routine planning use.

title: Modified atmosphere packaging extends raspberry shelf life for export
abstract: This study investigated the effect of modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) on the postharvest quality and shelf life of Serbian-grown raspberries intended for export markets. Three gas compositions — 5% O₂/15% CO₂/80% N₂, 10% O₂/10% CO₂/80% N₂, and ambient air control — were evaluated at 2 °C storage over a 14-day period. Quality parameters including firmness, color (L*, a*, b*), soluble solids content, titratable acidity, and visual mold incidence were monitored at two-day intervals. Microbiological analyses targeted total aerobic counts and Botrytis cinerea colony formation. Results demonstrated that the 5% O₂/15% CO₂ atmosphere reduced Botrytis incidence by 63% relative to control and maintained firmness above commercial acceptability thresholds for 12 days compared to 6 days in ambient conditions. Sensory panel scores for color and texture confirmed marketability at day 10 under optimal MAP conditions. The findings provide actionable gas-mix specifications for exporters shipping raspberries to Central European markets, and establish a data foundation for integrating MAP parameters into predictive shelf-life models. Practical recommendations for film permeability selection and pallet-level gas management are discussed.

title: Index Routing Policies for Multi-Tenant Search Services: A Simulation Study
abstract: Multi-tenant search services host thousands of independent indexes on shared infrastructure. Routing decisions—which node handles each index shard—affect both query latency and hardware utilisation. We simulate a 20-node cluster hosting 3,200 index shards with heterogeneous sizes and query-rate profiles drawn from anonymised access logs of a mid-sized document management platform. Four routing policies are compared: random placement, size-balanced bin packing, query-rate-aware placement, and a combined policy that jointly optimises for size and rate. The combined policy reduces 99th-percentile latency by 27% and lowers peak CPU utilisation by 19% relative to random placement under realistic diurnal load patterns. Simulation is implemented in a purpose-built discrete-event framework to allow reproducible experimentation without requiring access to production hardware. Sensitivity analyses show the gains hold across a range of shard-size distributions.

title: Transferability of Calibrated Macroscopic Model Parameters Between Comparable Corridor Types in the Western Balkans
abstract: A recurring practical constraint in regional transport studies is insufficient local traffic data for full model calibration. This paper investigates whether fundamental diagram parameters calibrated on well-monitored corridors in Vojvodina can be transferred to data-sparse corridors in northern Serbia and western Romania. Three donor corridors and four receiver corridors were identified on the basis of geometric similarity (lane count, design speed, access density) and traffic composition. Parameters from donor models were applied unchanged to receiver corridors; predicted AADT values were compared against periodic count data. The mean absolute percentage error of transferred parameters was 13.7%, compared to 6.2% for locally calibrated parameters. A weighted transfer procedure that adjusts for differences in truck share reduced the transferred-model error to 9.4%. The findings suggest that parameter transfer is acceptable for screening-level corridor assessments but should be supplemented by at least two weeks of local counting before detailed design studies.

title: Warm-Starting Metaheuristics Using Machine-Learning Predictions of Near-Optimal Depot Assignments
abstract: Metaheuristic solvers for multi-depot VRP instances often spend a significant fraction of their runtime escaping poor initial solutions. This paper investigates whether a gradient-boosted classifier trained on instance features can predict near-optimal depot assignments for individual tasks, thereby warm-starting the metaheuristic. A dataset of 4,800 solved MDVRPTW instances was used for training; features included task spatial coordinates, time-window midpoints, inter-depot distances, and task service durations. The classifier achieved a task-level assignment accuracy of 71.3% on held-out instances compared to optimal solutions. When used to initialise a tabu search, the ML-warm-started variants reached equivalent solution quality 38% faster than random initialisation and 19% faster than nearest-depot initialisation. Gains were largest on instances with high depot load imbalance. The paper also reports results on the public Cordeau MDVRP benchmark for comparability with existing literature.

title: A Tabu Search Approach for the Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing Problem with Hard Time Windows on Road Maintenance Networks
abstract: This paper presents a tabu search (TS) heuristic for scheduling maintenance crews across multiple depots on a regional road network. The test instances were derived from publicly available road segment data for Vojvodina, comprising 214 maintenance tasks distributed across six depot locations. Time windows were specified as four-hour intervals corresponding to low-traffic periods. The TS algorithm used a move-evaluation scheme based on segment-reinsertion and depot-reassignment operators, with a tenure list of 12 moves. Over 30 independent runs, the heuristic achieved solutions within 4.2% of a known lower bound obtained via LP relaxation. Total fleet travel distance was reduced by 18.3% compared to a nearest-neighbour baseline, while constraint violations fell to zero in all feasible instances. Computation times averaged 47 seconds on standard desktop hardware. The results suggest that moderate tabu tenure values outperform both short and long tenures in this problem class.

title: Modelling Maintenance Task Clustering for Geographically Dispersed Utility Networks Using K-Medoids Initialisation
abstract: Effective partitioning of maintenance tasks among depots is a prerequisite for tractable routing in large instances. This study evaluates three initialisation strategies—random assignment, nearest-depot assignment, and K-medoids clustering—as starting points for a variable neighbourhood search (VNS) on a synthetic benchmark set of 500 tasks across eight depots. Instances were generated using a spatial Poisson process calibrated to road density data from a 12,000 km² region in northern Serbia. K-medoids initialisation consistently produced better final solutions than the other two strategies, reducing total route cost by 9.1% on average across 15 benchmark groups. The paper also investigates how task density heterogeneity affects depot load balance, finding that uniform spatial distributions allow tighter workload constraints without significant cost penalties. Sensitivity analyses on time-window width (two to six hours) show a near-linear trade-off between fleet utilisation and feasibility rates.

title: Incorporating Skill Heterogeneity into Multi-Depot Routing for Road Infrastructure Repair Crews
abstract: Standard vehicle routing models assume homogeneous service capability across all vehicles. This paper extends the multi-depot VRP with time windows to account for crew skill levels, where each maintenance task requires one of three competence categories. The model was formulated as a mixed-integer linear programme (MILP) and solved with a branch-and-price algorithm for instances with up to 80 tasks and four depots. For larger instances (up to 320 tasks, six depots), a large neighbourhood search (LNS) heuristic was applied. Test data were drawn from maintenance records provided by a regional road authority in Serbia under a non-disclosure agreement. Results show that ignoring skill constraints leads to infeasible assignments in 23% of real-world instances examined; integrating skill matching increased total travel distance by only 6.8% compared to the unconstrained optimum. The LNS heuristic found solutions within 3.5% of the MILP optimum for instances where both were solvable.

title: Benchmark Set for Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing with Infrastructure Maintenance Constraints: Design and Baseline Results
abstract: Public benchmark libraries for VRP variants rarely capture characteristics specific to infrastructure maintenance: irregular task distribution along linear assets, mandatory service-window compliance, and multi-depot topology. This paper describes a benchmark set of 120 instances in four size tiers (50, 100, 200, and 400 tasks) constructed from a procedural generator that mimics road-network geometry. Each instance specifies depot locations, task positions, time windows, service durations, and vehicle capacities. Baseline results are reported for four algorithms: nearest-neighbour construction, Clarke–Wright savings, tabu search, and a genetic algorithm. Across all tiers, tabu search achieved the lowest average cost, but the genetic algorithm was more consistent on the largest tier. All instances and source code are published under a permissive open licence on an institutional repository. The benchmark is intended to support reproducible comparison of future algorithms addressing this problem class.

title: Real-Time Replanning of Maintenance Routes Under Unexpected Task Insertions: A Rolling-Horizon Framework
abstract: Infrastructure maintenance operations are frequently disrupted by urgent repair tasks that arise outside the original schedule. This paper proposes a rolling-horizon replanning framework in which the current routing solution is partially frozen and a reduced optimisation problem is solved over a look-ahead window of four to eight hours. The framework was implemented using a truncated branch-and-bound solver with a 30-second time limit per replanning cycle. Simulation experiments over a synthetic 12-hour workday with Poisson-distributed urgent task arrivals (mean rate 0.5 per hour) showed that the rolling-horizon approach reduced total overtime by 31% and task delay by 44% compared to a no-replanning baseline. Freezing 60% of already-committed vehicle assignments in each cycle provided the best balance between solution quality and computational feasibility. The paper also evaluates how the arrival rate of urgent tasks affects the benefit of shorter look-ahead windows.
venue: Journal of Scheduling and Logistics Research

title: GIS-Integrated Route Optimisation for Power Distribution Network Inspection in the Pannonian Region
abstract: Power distribution utilities operate geographically dispersed inspection fleets with strict scheduling requirements tied to grid load cycles. This study integrates a GIS data pipeline with a multi-depot routing solver to optimise inspection tours for 17 substations across a 9,400 km² service area in northern Serbia and southern Hungary. Road network travel times were extracted from a customised OpenStreetMap export, updated with seasonal speed profiles derived from traffic count data at 42 monitoring stations. A simulated annealing algorithm produced inspection schedules respecting both time-window and crew rest-period regulations. The optimised schedules reduced total vehicle-kilometres by 14.7% and eliminated all time-window violations present in the manually planned baseline. A sensitivity analysis demonstrates that a 15% increase in crew rest requirements raises total distance by only 3.2%, suggesting that regulatory tightening would have a modest operational impact for this operator.

title: Column Generation for Multi-Depot Maintenance Routing with Staggered Shift Starts
abstract: Many maintenance organisations stagger crew departure times to reduce peak depot congestion and improve service coverage. This paper incorporates staggered shift starts into a multi-depot VRP formulation by introducing a set of permissible departure time slots at each depot. The problem is solved via column generation, where the pricing subproblem is a shortest-path problem with time-window and capacity constraints solved by a bi-directional label-setting algorithm. The master problem was implemented in CPLEX 20.1. Tests on 40 instances derived from the benchmark set introduced in the authors' earlier work show that incorporating staggered starts reduces peak congestion indicators by up to 27% with an average cost increase of only 4.1%. The column generation approach solved instances of up to 150 tasks to optimality within 10 minutes; beyond 200 tasks a heuristic column selection strategy was necessary, yielding solutions within 5% of lower bounds.

title: Optimisation of Winter Road Maintenance Fleets Across Multiple Depots: A Case Study in Vojvodina
abstract: Winter maintenance of regional roads imposes tight response-time requirements and spatially concentrated demand during precipitation events. This chapter examines how multi-depot VRP models can be calibrated to winter maintenance operations by combining meteorological forecast data with pavement condition indices. Historical weather data from 11 automatic stations in Vojvodina covering five winter seasons (2017–2022) were used to construct probabilistic task arrival models. A scenario-based robust optimisation approach generated depot staffing and pre-positioning recommendations that performed within 8% of the deterministic optimum across 80% of simulated weather scenarios. The chapter discusses practical barriers to implementation, including dispatcher acceptance of algorithm-generated plans and the absence of real-time vehicle telemetry in most Serbian public road companies. Recommendations for phased adoption are outlined, with cost-benefit estimates for a medium-sized regional operator managing 22 vehicles from three depots.

title: Fleet Electrification and Route Feasibility in Multi-Depot Maintenance Operations: Range Constraints and Charging Stop Integration
abstract: Replacing diesel maintenance vehicles with battery-electric equivalents introduces range and charging constraints that interact with existing time-window requirements. This preprint formulates the multi-depot electric VRP with time windows and partial charging stops (MDEVRPTW-PC) and proposes an adaptive large neighbourhood search (ALNS) to solve it. Charging infrastructure is modelled using publicly available data on fast-charging stations in Serbia and Hungary. Experiments compare the all-diesel baseline, a partial electrification scenario (50% of fleet), and a full electrification scenario across 30 real-derived instances. Full electrification increases total route cost by 22–35% depending on task distribution and available charging density, while a 50% partial scenario increases cost by 8–13%. The paper identifies geographic corridors where charging gaps would require route redesign even with moderate task density, providing input for charging infrastructure placement planning.

title: Application of principal component analysis to fault detection in fluid-bed coating: a case study with enteric polymer dispersions
abstract: This study examined the use of principal component analysis (PCA) applied to routinely collected process variables—inlet air temperature, exhaust air temperature, product temperature, spray rate, atomisation air pressure, and pan speed—for fault detection during enteric coating of 5 mm acetaminophen tablets in a 3-litre Glatt GPCG-1 fluidised-bed coater. Reference batches (n = 18) were used to build a PCA model, and Hotelling's T² and Q-statistic control charts were computed for 24 additional batches including six deliberately perturbed runs with introduced deviations in spray rate (±25%) and atomisation air pressure (±15%). The T² chart detected all six perturbed batches, with out-of-control signals appearing within 3–7 minutes of the perturbation onset. False alarm rates on normal batches were 4.2% at the 95% confidence limit. Results support the use of standard process variable PCA monitoring as a complementary tool to spectroscopic methods in resource-limited production environments.

title: Box–Behnken design optimisation of coating suspension composition and process parameters for sustained-release pellet coating
abstract: A Box–Behnken design with 15 experimental runs was used to optimise three formulation variables—ethylcellulose-to-hydroxypropyl methylcellulose ratio (70:30–90:10), plasticiser level (5–15% w/w relative to polymer), and coating level (5–15% weight gain)—alongside two process variables: inlet air temperature (35–55 °C) and spray rate (5–15 g/min), for sustained-release coating of 500–600 µm theophylline pellets. Drug release at 1 h, 4 h, and 8 h in phosphate buffer pH 6.8 was used as the response. Response surface models showed significant main effects of coating level and polymer ratio on the 1 h release (R² = 0.94), with a strong interaction between plasticiser level and inlet air temperature at 4 h. Optimised conditions predicted 18.7% release at 1 h, 52.3% at 4 h, and 89.1% at 8 h; experimental verification batches (n = 3) yielded values within 3.4% of predictions. Desirability function composite optimisation was used for multi-response optimisation.

title: Extrusion–spheronisation of microcrystalline cellulose–calcium hydrogen phosphate pellets: influence of wet mass consistency on pellet size distribution and drug loading uniformity
abstract: Pellets intended as multiparticulate drug carriers were manufactured by extrusion–spheronisation using binary MCC–CaHPO4 blends (MCC fraction 40–80% w/w). A 3% w/v hydroxypropyl cellulose solution was used as binder. Wet mass water content was varied between 28 and 44% to modulate extrudate plasticity. Pellet size distributions were characterised by laser diffraction (n = 3 batches per condition), and drug loading uniformity of theophylline was assessed by assaying 10 individual pellets per batch by HPLC. MCC fraction of 60% and water content of 36% yielded the narrowest size distribution (D10/D90 ratio = 0.64) and highest uniformity (RSD < 3.2% for theophylline content). Increasing CaHPO4 content beyond 40% resulted in bimodal size distributions attributable to incomplete plasticity. Scanning electron microscopy confirmed smooth, near-spherical morphology under optimal conditions. The data provide quantitative guidance for binder selection and water addition in pellet manufacturing.

title: Swelling and erosion behaviour of hydroxypropyl methylcellulose matrix tablets: effect of polymer viscosity grade and drug solubility
abstract: Hydrophilic matrix tablets prepared with three HPMC viscosity grades (K4M, K15M, K100M) and two model drugs of contrasting aqueous solubility (metoprolol succinate and ibuprofen) were characterised with respect to tablet swelling, gel layer thickness and erosion rate using digital image analysis at 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 h time points in USP Apparatus II at 50 rpm, 900 mL of pH 6.8 phosphate buffer. Gel front and erosion front positions were quantified for 12 formulation variants (n = 6 per variant). HPMC K100M produced the thickest gel layer (up to 2.8 mm at 6 h) and slowest erosion for both drugs. Drug solubility significantly modulated the contribution of diffusion versus erosion: for metoprolol succinate, erosion accounted for approximately 65% of total release at 8 h, compared with 38% for ibuprofen under identical polymer loading. A combined diffusion–erosion model fitted the experimental profiles with mean absolute percentage errors below 8% in all cases. The results confirm that polymer viscosity grade and drug solubility must be considered simultaneously when predicting mechanism-dominant release.

title: Примена Box-Behnken дизајна у оптимизацији хидрофилних матрикс таблета с контролисаним ослобађањем метформин хидрохлорида
abstract: У раду је приказана примена Box-Behnken експерименталног дизајна за оптимизацију формулације матрикс таблета с контролисаним ослобађањем метформин хидрохлорида. Независне варијабле биле су удео HPMC K15M (10–30% m/m), удео карбопола 971P (1–5% m/m) и сила компресије (8–16 kN). Зависне варијабле обухватале су: проценат ослобађања лека за 1, 4 и 8 часова (USP апарат II, 0,1 М HCl / pH 6,8 фосфатни пуфер), тврдоћу таблете и фриабилитет. Добијени резултати обрађени су методом одзивне površine, а оптимална формулација предвиђена моделом потврђена је експериментом (одступање < 5%). Оптималне вредности независних варијабли износиле су 22% HPMC, 3% карбопола и 12 kN. Профил ослобађања оптималне формулације задовољио је критеријум f2 ≥ 50 у поређењу са референтним препаратом.

title: Mechanistic dissolution modelling of HPMC matrix tablets using a moving-boundary diffusion–erosion framework: parameter estimation and predictive validation
abstract: A one-dimensional moving-boundary model describing simultaneous gel swelling, drug diffusion through the hydrated layer, and polymer erosion was implemented in MATLAB and fitted to in vitro dissolution datasets for six HPMC K15M matrix formulations containing drugs spanning a 500-fold solubility range (0.04–20 mg/mL). Model parameters—effective diffusivity, erosion rate constant, and gel–solvent interface velocity—were estimated by nonlinear least-squares optimisation against USP Apparatus II profiles collected at three pH values (1.2, 4.5, 6.8). Leave-one-out cross-validation demonstrated that the model predicts withheld dissolution profiles with root-mean-square error ≤ 6.2% across all tested conditions. Sensitivity analysis identified gel-layer diffusivity and erosion rate constant as the parameters with highest influence on the 50% dissolution time (t50), accounting collectively for over 80% of variance in a Sobol first-order analysis. The parameterised model was subsequently used in forward simulations to screen 120 virtual formulation variants, identifying compositions predicted to achieve 12-h sustained release targets, thereby illustrating its utility as a formulation design tool.

title: Ethylcellulose film coating of theophylline pellets in a laboratory-scale fluidised bed: coating thickness, porosity and in vitro release
abstract: Theophylline pellets (250–355 µm fraction) produced by extrusion–spheronisation were coated with ethylcellulose (Surelease dispersion, 15% w/w solids) in a Wurster fluidised-bed coater at coating level targets of 5, 10, 15, and 20% w/w. Coating thickness was measured by cross-sectional SEM image analysis (20 pellets per batch). Membrane porosity was assessed by mercury intrusion porosimetry. In vitro release was carried out in USP Apparatus III (dip speed 10 dpm) in pH 1.2 HCl for 2 h followed by pH 6.8 phosphate buffer for 10 h. Coating level of 15% produced a mean membrane thickness of 14.2 µm and sustained release over 12 h with zero-order kinetics (R² = 0.997). At 20% coating, pore closure was evident (porosity 0.8% vs 4.1% at 10%) and release slowed unacceptably to 58% at 12 h. A permeability model relating porosity to release rate constant was developed and validated against independent batches with mean prediction error of 9.3%.

title: In vitro–in vivo correlation (IVIVC) for sustained-release HPMC matrix tablets: a Level A correlation using deconvolution and absorption modelling
abstract: A Level A IVIVC was developed for sustained-release metoprolol succinate HPMC K100M matrix tablets using in vitro dissolution data from USP Apparatus II (pH 6.8, 75 rpm) and published in vivo plasma concentration–time profiles from an open-label crossover study in 12 healthy volunteers. Numerical deconvolution (Wagner–Nelson method) was used to estimate in vivo drug input rates, and a one-compartment absorption model was applied to parameterise the in vivo dissolution process. The in vitro–in vivo time scaling factor was 1.18, indicating moderately faster in vitro release. The resulting IVIVC demonstrated R² = 0.963 between predicted and observed Cmax and AUC0–12h across five formulation variants differing in HPMC content (15–35% w/w). Internal predictability was assessed: mean prediction errors were 7.8% for Cmax and 5.4% for AUC, within FDA Guidance thresholds. The established correlation was used to set dissolution specifications bracketing the in vivo-relevant release window.

title: Dissolution model-informed design space definition for HPMC matrix tablets: a Quality by Design case study
abstract: A mechanistic dissolution model, previously validated for HPMC K15M matrices, was integrated into a QbD design space definition exercise for a once-daily sustained-release tablet containing a BCS Class II drug (simulated solubility 0.12 mg/mL at pH 6.8). Critical material attributes (HPMC viscosity grade, drug particle size d50) and critical process parameters (compaction pressure, granulation endpoint) were propagated through the model to predict their combined effect on the dissolution design space. Monte Carlo simulations (10,000 runs) were used to map the probability of meeting the dissolution acceptance criteria (Q ≥ 70% at 12 h) across the factor space. A proven acceptable range was identified where HPMC K15M content between 20–28%, drug d50 between 25–60 µm, and compaction force between 10–15 kN yielded > 95% probability of compliance. The approach was prospectively confirmed by manufacturing and testing 18 verification batches; 17 met specifications. The study illustrates how mechanistic modelling can reduce the experimental burden in early formulation development.

title: Comparative dissolution behaviour of generic and reference sustained-release doxazosin mesylate matrix tablets marketed in the Western Balkans: f2 analysis and mechanistic interpretation
abstract: Seven sustained-release doxazosin mesylate 4 mg matrix tablet products available on pharmacy markets in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia were subjected to comparative dissolution testing using USP Apparatus II (50 rpm, 900 mL, pH 6.8 phosphate buffer, 37 °C) at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 12 h (n = 12 per product). Similarity factors (f2) were calculated against the reference product. Three generics failed the f2 ≥ 50 similarity criterion, releasing ≥ 85% drug within 6 h compared with 62% for the reference. Scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy of tablet cross-sections revealed differences in polymer distribution and particle morphology consistent with varying HPMC grades. Application of the mechanistic diffusion–erosion model to the failing generics indicated that erosion rate constants two- to threefold higher than the reference product explained the accelerated release. The findings highlight the need for mechanistic dissolution testing protocols in generic approval processes in the region.

title: Predicting the effect of pellet size and coating thickness on in vitro dissolution from multiparticulate capsules using a distributed-parameter model
abstract: A distributed-parameter mathematical model was developed to describe drug release from a population of coated pellets enclosed in a hard gelatin capsule, accounting for variability in pellet diameter (log-normal distribution, σ = 0.08–0.22) and ethylcellulose membrane thickness (CV = 5–18%). The model treated each pellet as an independent diffusion cell and summed contributions weighted by the respective size and thickness distributions, which were characterised experimentally by laser diffraction and confocal microscopy on three independent batches of diclofenac sodium pellets. Model predictions were compared with USP Apparatus III dissolution profiles (10 dpm, pH 6.8, 37 °C). The model reproduced the dissolution curves with RMSE < 5.4% across all batches without re-fitting. Sensitivity analysis showed that membrane thickness CV was the dominant source of dissolution variability: reducing CV from 18 to 8% narrowed the predicted 80% dissolution time interval from ±1.8 to ±0.6 h. These findings support tighter process control targets for coating uniformity in pellet manufacturing.

title: Fractionation of pumpkin seed oil phospholipids using supercritical CO₂ modified with ethanol as co-solvent
abstract: Phospholipids in pumpkin seed oil represent a minor but functionally important fraction with relevance for liposomal drug delivery systems. Crude pumpkin seed oil, obtained by cold pressing, was subjected to supercritical CO₂ fractionation at pressures between 200 and 350 bar and temperatures between 45 and 65 °C, with ethanol added as co-solvent at 2, 5, and 8 mol%. Phospholipid content in the fractions was quantified by HPLC-DAD after derivatisation, and thin-layer chromatography was used for class identification. At 250 bar, 55 °C, and 5 mol% ethanol, phosphatidylcholine concentration in the enriched fraction reached 42.3 mg/g, compared to 11.7 mg/g in the starting oil. Increasing co-solvent concentration beyond 5 mol% led to co-extraction of neutral lipids, reducing selectivity. The study provides a solvent-free route to phospholipid-enriched fractions without the use of hexane or acetone, which is relevant for nutraceutical and cosmeceutical applications requiring clean-label ingredients.

title: Mathematical modelling of supercritical CO₂ extraction of fixed oil from grape seeds: broken-and-intact cell model applied to pilot-scale data
abstract: Scale-up from laboratory to pilot extraction requires reliable mathematical models to predict extraction kinetics and design operating schedules. This work applied the broken-and-intact cell (BIC) model to describe the supercritical CO₂ extraction of grape seed oil at pilot scale (5 L vessel, 2.5 kg charge, 350 bar, 50 °C). Extraction curves were obtained at three CO₂ flow rates (10, 20, and 30 kg/h) and the BIC model was fitted using nonlinear least-squares regression. Model parameters—broken cell fraction, mass transfer coefficient in intact cells, and axial dispersion coefficient—were estimated with 95% confidence intervals. Predicted extraction curves matched experimental data with root mean square errors below 4.2% across all flow rates. The fitted model was used to simulate optimal extraction time for 95% yield recovery, predicting a minimum solvent-to-feed ratio of 28 kg CO₂/kg feed. Grape seed oil fatty acid composition (predominantly linoleic acid, 68–71%) was consistent across scales. The validated model is intended as a tool for process design at industrial scale.

title: The Establishment of the Administrative Court of Serbia (2010): Legislative Choices and Inherited Deficits
abstract: Serbia's Administrative Court, created by the Law on Administrative Disputes of 2009 and fully operational from 1 January 2010, represented the first dedicated administrative court in the country since the interwar period. This article analyses the parliamentary record, comparative law memoranda prepared by the Ministry of Justice, and the court's published statistics from its first three years of operation (2010–2012). The article identifies three structural choices—single-instance jurisdiction, limited cassation-only review, and the exclusion of urgency procedures—that reflect path-dependent influences from the Yugoslav period and fiscal constraints, rather than from the EU administrative justice models that were formally cited during the reform process. Case-load data show that by end-2012 the court had a backlog of approximately 23,000 unresolved cases, already nearly double its annual throughput capacity. The article argues that the reform achieved formal institutional separation without resolving the functional weaknesses of administrative adjudication.

title: Administrative Dispute Resolution in North Macedonia: Reforms Under EU Candidate Pressure, 2005–2022
abstract: This article examines the trajectory of administrative justice reform in North Macedonia from the country's EU candidate status (2005) to the opening of accession negotiations (2022), with particular attention to the 2010 and 2019 amendments to the Law on Administrative Disputes. Using official EU Progress Reports, National Programme for Adoption of the Acquis documents, Parliamentary Assembly records, and interviews with five administrative judges at the Administrative Court in Skopje, the study assesses the extent to which EU conditionality shaped the pace and content of reform. The analysis finds that the shift from single-tier cassation review to a two-tier system with elements of full jurisdiction in 2019 was directly linked to Chapter 23 benchmarks in the EU negotiation framework, yet implementation remained incomplete at the time of writing, with the Higher Administrative Court becoming operational only in 2021. The article situates North Macedonia within the broader pattern of externally driven but domestically contested administrative justice reform in the Western Balkans.
venue: Review of Central and East European Law

title: Discretionary Power and Rule-Bound Decision-Making in Serbian Administrative Law: A Comparative Survey
abstract: This article examines the boundaries of administrative discretion in Serbian public law by comparing the domestic framework with those of Hungary, Croatia, and Austria. The study draws on a corpus of 340 administrative court decisions issued between 2000 and 2009, coded against a set of 18 criteria relating to the scope and intensity of judicial review. Results show that Serbian administrative courts apply a narrower standard of proportionality review than their Austrian counterparts, leaving a wider unreviewable discretionary zone for executive bodies. The article argues that this gap carries implications for the legality of rule-based automated systems if they are introduced to support administrative decisions without corresponding judicial oversight reform. The analysis employs qualitative legal comparison alongside a simple quantitative coding scheme applied to the case-law sample, and concludes with concrete recommendations for legislative amendment to the Law on General Administrative Procedure.

title: Transparency Obligations for AI-Assisted Decisions in Serbian Administrative Law: De Lege Lata and De Lege Ferenda
abstract: This article analyses the current state of Serbian administrative law with respect to transparency obligations that would apply if public bodies were to deploy AI-assisted decision-making systems. The de lege lata analysis covers the Law on General Administrative Procedure (2016), the Law on Personal Data Protection (2018), and the Law on Electronic Administration (2021), identifying provisions that impose or imply transparency requirements. The de lege ferenda analysis uses the EU Artificial Intelligence Act as a benchmark to identify gaps requiring legislative action. The study finds four significant gaps: absence of a duty to notify individuals that a decision was AI-assisted; absence of a requirement to publish the categories of AI systems in use; absence of a structured human review procedure; and absence of a mechanism for communicating system accuracy limitations to affected parties. Draft legislative amendments addressing each gap are set out in an annex.

title: The Right to an Explanation in Administrative Decision-Making: Lessons from French and German Practice for Serbian Reform
abstract: Drawing on the administrative procedure reforms introduced in France (2015 Loi pour une République numérique) and Germany (amendments to the Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz), this book chapter analyses what a statutory duty to explain automated decisions would require in the Serbian legal context. The chapter proceeds in three parts: first, a doctrinal reconstruction of the explanation requirement as it has developed in French and German administrative law and case-law; second, an assessment of whether existing Serbian administrative procedure law contains latent equivalents; third, a legislative drafting exercise producing a model provision. The chapter concludes that Serbian law already contains a general duty to state reasons for administrative acts that could be extended by analogy, but that this extension requires an explicit legislative signal to be reliable in practice. Particular attention is paid to the tension between the duty to explain and trade secret protections invoked by private technology vendors supplying software to public bodies.

title: Profiling in Public Administration: Data Protection Law Meets Administrative Procedure in the Western Balkans
abstract: This article examines the intersection between personal data protection rules derived from the Council of Europe Convention 108 and the GDPR, and administrative procedure obligations, in the context of profiling practices used by social welfare and tax authorities in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia. The empirical basis consists of 22 semi-structured interviews with public officials in the three countries conducted in 2016, supplemented by freedom-of-information requests yielding internal policy documents. The study finds that none of the three jurisdictions had produced formal internal guidance on how profiling-based risk scores should be integrated into decision workflows in a manner consistent with individual procedural rights. The article maps the specific normative gaps and argues that the EU GDPR Article 22 framework, although not directly applicable in the Western Balkans, provides a useful template for national legislators.

title: Technical Documentation as a Legal Instrument: What the GDPR Record-Keeping Obligation Tells Us About Future AI Regulation
abstract: Article 30 of the GDPR requires controllers to maintain records of processing activities, and supervisory authority guidance has gradually expanded the substantive content those records must contain. This article analyses decisions and guidance issued by ten European data protection authorities between 2018 and 2020 to determine what a mature technical documentation obligation looks like in practice. Using content analysis of 87 enforcement decisions and 34 guidance documents, the study codes the types of information authorities consistently demand, the format requirements they impose, and the evidentiary use they make of records in proceedings. The results identify eight recurring documentation elements—including data flows, retention schedules, processor contracts, and security measures—that appear in at least 70 per cent of the sampled materials. The article argues that this established GDPR practice constitutes a model for the technical documentation requirements later incorporated into the EU Artificial Intelligence Act for high-risk systems, and evaluates the continuities and divergences between the two regimes.

title: High-Risk AI Systems in Public Administration: Mapping the Operators' Obligations Under the Proposed EU AI Act
abstract: Presented at the 2021 International Conference on Administrative Law and Digital Technologies in Ljubljana, this paper provides a systematic mapping of the compliance obligations that the then-proposed EU Artificial Intelligence Act would impose on public bodies acting as operators of high-risk AI systems. The analysis focuses on the obligations in Articles 29 and 30 of the Commission's April 2021 proposal, examining: the duty to follow the supplier's instructions of use; the duty to monitor system performance; the duty to suspend the system in case of serious incident; and the duty to cooperate with national supervisory authorities. For each obligation the paper identifies the corresponding administrative law doctrine—duty of care, proportionality, good administration—and assesses whether existing administrative procedure laws in Serbia and the EU Member States adequately operationalise them. The paper concludes by identifying three obligations that require new procedural instruments not currently present in most national legal systems.

title: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for Algorithmic Systems: Designing a Procedural Model for Public Bodies
abstract: This article develops a procedural model for fundamental rights impact assessments (FRIA) as required under Article 29a of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act as amended by the European Parliament in 2023. The model is constructed by synthesising three existing assessment frameworks: the data protection impact assessment procedure under GDPR Article 35, the equality impact assessment practice developed in the United Kingdom, and the human rights due diligence methodology promoted by the Council of Europe. The article identifies seven procedural steps—scoping, stakeholder mapping, rights inventory, likelihood and severity scoring, mitigation design, residual risk acceptance, and periodic review—and evaluates each against the specific requirements of the AI Act text and the fundamental rights protected under the EU Charter. A draft template is provided as an appendix, calibrated to the resources available to medium-sized public bodies. The article does not assert that the proposed model satisfies all future regulatory guidance, which remains to be issued.

title: Conformity Assessment Procedures Under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act: An Administrative Law Reading
abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act establishes conformity assessment procedures that must be completed before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service. This book chapter examines those procedures through the lens of administrative law, treating them as a form of preventive administrative authorisation. The chapter proceeds in four parts. First, it situates conformity assessment within the broader tradition of pre-market authorisation in EU product safety law. Second, it analyses the internal conformity assessment procedure applicable to most high-risk systems under Annex VI, identifying its evidentiary and documentary requirements. Third, it examines the third-party notified body procedure applicable to biometric and critical infrastructure systems. Fourth, it considers the enforcement consequences of non-compliance, including market withdrawal and prohibition orders issued by national market surveillance authorities. The chapter argues that the notified body procedure creates a hybrid public-private regulatory arrangement without adequate public law accountability mechanisms.

title: Post-Market Monitoring Obligations for High-Risk AI Systems: Compliance Costs and Legal Uncertainty for Small Public Bodies
abstract: Article 72 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act requires operators of high-risk AI systems to implement post-market monitoring plans and report serious incidents to national authorities. This article evaluates the practical compliance burden of these obligations for small and medium-sized public bodies—defined here as municipal administrations and social welfare agencies with fewer than 200 staff. The study is based on a survey administered in 2023 to 64 such bodies in Serbia, Hungary, and Romania, supplemented by 15 in-depth interviews with heads of legal and IT departments. Results show that 81 per cent of respondents lacked dedicated staff capable of drafting a monitoring plan compliant with the Act's requirements, and 74 per cent were unaware of the incident-reporting timelines. The article identifies three structural causes of under-preparedness—resource constraints, cross-functional coordination failures, and lack of regulatory guidance—and proposes differentiated compliance pathways for bodies below a defined resource threshold.

title: The Role of National Competent Authorities Under the EU AI Act: Institutional Design Choices for Western Balkan Candidates
abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act requires each Member State to designate one or more national competent authorities responsible for implementation and enforcement. This article examines the institutional design choices made by five EU Member States that published their designation decisions in 2024—Austria, the Netherlands, Portugal, Finland, and Estonia—and draws lessons for Western Balkan candidate countries preparing alignment legislation. The comparison covers: the choice between a dedicated AI authority, an expanded data protection authority, and a sectoral regulator model; the scope of investigative and sanctioning powers; coordination mechanisms with the European AI Office; and resource allocation. Serbia is used as the primary case study for the candidate-country analysis, given its advanced EU integration status and the existence of a draft AI alignment strategy published by the government in 2023. The article argues that Serbia should opt for an expanded mandate within the existing Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection rather than creating a new body.

title: Human Oversight Requirements in the EU AI Act: Between Formal Compliance and Effective Control
abstract: Articles 14 and 29 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act impose human oversight requirements on providers and operators of high-risk AI systems, but the Act provides little guidance on what effective oversight entails in operational settings. This article analyses the human oversight requirement by drawing on organisational theory, administrative law doctrine, and empirical case studies of three public-sector deployments of algorithmic systems: a child welfare risk assessment tool used by a regional social services agency in Germany, a benefits eligibility screening tool used by a national social insurance fund in a Central European country, and a document classification system used by a European customs authority. For each case, the article reconstructs the oversight arrangements actually in place and evaluates them against the Act's text and recitals. The analysis finds a recurrent pattern in which oversight is nominally present but operationally ineffective because reviewers lack both the time and the technical literacy to meaningfully assess system outputs.

title: Liability for Automated Administrative Decisions Under Serbian Law: Current Framework and the Case for Statutory Reform
abstract: This article examines the state liability framework applicable when automated or AI-assisted administrative decisions cause harm to individuals under Serbian law. The doctrinal analysis covers the constitutional basis for state liability (Article 35 of the Constitution), the general tort provisions of the Law on Obligations, and the specific administrative liability rules in the Law on General Administrative Procedure. The article identifies two scenarios that the current framework handles poorly: harm caused by a technically correct decision that nonetheless produces disproportionate effects on an individual due to reliance on an inaccurate training dataset, and harm caused by a decision that would have been revised had a human reviewer actually examined the AI system's output rather than accepting it automatically. For each scenario, the article assesses whether existing fault, unlawfulness, and causation doctrines can accommodate the claim, concluding that the causation analysis is the most problematic element in both cases. Legislative reform options are presented and evaluated.

title: Regulatory Sandboxes for AI Under the EU AI Act: Public Law Constraints and Opportunities for Candidate Countries
abstract: Articles 57 to 63 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act establish a framework for national regulatory sandboxes in which AI systems can be developed and tested under relaxed compliance conditions. This article analyses the public law constraints that apply to such sandboxes—legality, equal treatment, proportionality, and accountability—and assesses whether the Act's framework adequately respects those constraints. The analysis then considers the specific position of EU candidate countries, which are encouraged under the Act's recitals to establish compatible sandbox regimes in preparation for accession. Using Serbia as the central example, the article examines whether the existing Serbian legal framework for administrative experimentation—sparse as it is—provides a sufficient basis for establishing a compliant sandbox, or whether primary legislation is required. The article concludes that a sandbox ordinance adopted by the Government under existing enabling legislation would be legally sufficient but institutionally fragile, and that a dedicated statutory instrument would be preferable.

title: Sub-legislative Rulemaking and the EU Approximation Agenda: Constitutional Tensions in Western Balkan Candidate States
abstract: European Union accession requires candidate states to transpose a large body of technical acquis, much of which is implemented not through primary legislation but through agency rulebooks and adopted European standards. This book chapter examines how this external normative pressure interacts with constitutional norms on delegated legislation in Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and North Macedonia. Based on a review of 118 transposition instruments across the three states covering the period 2012–2018, the chapter identifies a structural tension: EU-driven technical rulemaking expands agency norm-production at a pace that domestic constitutional frameworks, designed for a different scale of regulation, struggle to accommodate. The chapter maps the gap between formal constitutional requirements and actual legislative practice, and surveys judicial responses where they exist. Recommendations are addressed to both domestic legislators and EU technical assistance programmes.

title: Partition-Aware Inverted Index Construction for Heterogeneous Document Streams
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of building inverted indexes over document streams that vary widely in language, length, and encoding. We propose a partition-aware construction algorithm that assigns incoming documents to index shards based on a lightweight language-and-length feature hash, reducing cross-shard query fan-out by approximately 34% compared to round-robin partitioning on a corpus of 12 million news articles drawn from four Balkan-language feeds. Index build time on a six-node cluster decreased by 18% while median query latency fell from 47 ms to 31 ms at the 50th percentile. The approach requires no prior knowledge of the full corpus distribution and adapts incrementally as stream statistics shift. Experiments use Apache Lucene as the underlying segment engine, with a custom coordinator layer implemented in Java. Recall at rank 10 remains within 0.4% of a monolithic baseline.
