title: Monitoring moisture content during aqueous pan coating of sugar spheres using near-infrared diffuse reflectance spectroscopy
abstract: Near-infrared (NIR) diffuse reflectance spectroscopy was evaluated as an in-line tool for monitoring moisture content during aqueous hydroxypropyl methylcellulose coating of 700–850 µm sugar spheres in a 10-litre side-vented pan coater. Calibration models were developed using partial least squares regression on spectra collected at 30-second intervals throughout 12 coating runs at varying spray rates (4–12 g/min) and inlet air temperatures (40–60 °C). The final PLS model achieved a root mean square error of cross-validation of 0.18% w/w moisture, validated against Karl Fischer titration on pulled samples. Score plots from principal component analysis of the spectral data clearly separated runs with suboptimal drying from those operating within target ranges. The approach enabled detection of a moisture accumulation event in three of twelve runs approximately 8 minutes before visible tablet agglomeration occurred, demonstrating the utility of in-line NIR for early fault detection in pan coating.

title: Multivariate statistical process control applied to solid dosage film-coating: a review of methods and industrial case studies
abstract: This book chapter surveys the application of multivariate statistical process control (MSPC) to film-coating unit operations in solid dosage manufacturing, covering the period 2000–2015. Methods reviewed include PCA-based monitoring charts, partial least squares discriminant analysis for batch end-point determination, and multi-way PCA for batch trajectory analysis. Industrial case studies drawn from the peer-reviewed literature are categorised by coating type (aqueous, organic solvent, hot-melt), equipment scale (laboratory to production), and the source of process data (online sensors, at-line spectroscopy, or historian process variables). The chapter discusses practical implementation challenges including the choice of reference batch set size, time-alignment of batch trajectories with dynamic time warping, and the interpretability of latent variable models for operators unfamiliar with multivariate methods. Gaps identified include limited published data on scale-up transitions and on coatings applied to non-spherical substrates.

title: Comparison of D-optimal and full factorial designs for characterising the effect of pan coating process variables on tablet weight gain variability
abstract: Weight gain variability across individual tablets is a critical quality attribute in film coating, yet the relative efficiency of different experimental designs for characterising its dependence on process parameters has received limited systematic attention. This study compared a 2⁴ full factorial design (16 runs) with a D-optimal design (12 runs) constructed in the same four-factor space—inlet air temperature (45–65 °C), pan speed (8–16 rpm), spray rate (6–14 g/min), and coating suspension solids content (10–20% w/w)—for aqueous HPMC coating of 300 mg placebo tablets in a 15-litre pan coater. Weight gain relative standard deviation (RSD) across 20 tablets per batch end-point was the response. Prediction variance maps and model coefficient confidence intervals from both designs were compared. The D-optimal design recovered 94% of the prediction accuracy of the full factorial at 75% of the experimental effort. Pan speed and spray rate showed the largest main effects on RSD (p < 0.01), and their interaction term was statistically significant in both designs.

title: Raman spectroscopy for in-line coating thickness estimation on film-coated tablets: calibration strategy and prediction uncertainty
abstract: In-line Raman spectroscopy was investigated as a non-destructive method for estimating mean coating thickness on film-coated 400 mg ibuprofen tablets during aqueous ethylcellulose coating in a side-vented pan coater at the 6-litre scale. Spectra were collected every 60 seconds using a PharmaScan PB-2 immersion probe (invented instrument). A PLS calibration model was trained on 220 spectra from 11 reference batches spanning coating thickness values of 30–180 µm (confirmed by cross-sectional optical microscopy on pulled samples). The RMSECV for coating thickness was 8.3 µm on a leave-one-batch-out cross-validation scheme. Prediction uncertainty was decomposed into contributions from model error, spectral noise, and batch-to-batch variability using a Monte Carlo resampling approach (5000 iterations). Results indicated that batch-to-batch variability in tablet core composition accounted for 38% of total prediction uncertainty, suggesting that incorporating core spectral pre-processing could further improve model robustness across manufacturing campaigns.

title: Batch trajectory analysis with multi-way PCA for monitoring scale-dependent coating dynamics in side-vented pan coaters
abstract: Scale-up of film-coating processes often introduces changes in batch trajectory shape that invalidate monitoring models built at smaller scale. This study applied multi-way principal component analysis (MPCA) to batch process data from aqueous HPMC coating runs conducted at three pan scales: 6-litre (n = 14 batches), 30-litre (n = 11 batches), and 120-litre (n = 9 batches). Time-alignment across batches was performed using indicator variable synchronisation based on cumulative spray volume. Five process variables were monitored per run. Score trajectories on PC1–PC2 showed systematic between-scale shifts attributable primarily to differences in exhaust air humidity dynamics, confirmed by contribution plots. A two-step monitoring strategy was proposed in which a scale-specific MPCA model is used for real-time fault detection and a cross-scale PLS model is used for end-point prediction. Cross-validated root mean square errors for weight gain prediction at the 120-litre scale were 0.43% using the cross-scale model, compared to 1.12% when the 6-litre model was applied directly.

title: Central composite design study of fluidised-bed coating variables affecting particle size distribution and friability of coated microcrystalline cellulose beads
abstract: A face-centred central composite design was used to investigate the effects of four process variables—inlet air temperature (40–60 °C), fluidisation air volume (30–50 m³/h), spray rate (3–9 g/min), and atomisation air pressure (1.2–2.0 bar)—on particle size distribution (d10, d50, d90, span) and friability of aqueous Eudragit RS 30D-coated microcrystalline cellulose beads at 10% weight gain in a 3-litre Glatt GPCG-1. Twenty-six experimental runs were conducted; responses were measured in triplicate. Quadratic regression models for d50 and span showed R² values of 0.91 and 0.87 respectively. Inlet air temperature and atomisation pressure had the strongest influence on span (p < 0.001), suggesting that droplet evaporation rate relative to deposition rate governs size distribution broadening. Friability was below 0.5% in all runs except two with low inlet temperature and high spray rate, where visible agglomeration increased friability to 1.8–2.3%. Overlay plots identified a feasible operating region satisfying all acceptance criteria simultaneously.

title: Sensitivity of coating end-point detection to reference batch selection in multivariate batch monitoring: a simulation study
abstract: The performance of multivariate batch monitoring models for coating end-point detection depends critically on the quality and representativeness of the reference batch set, yet systematic guidance on reference batch selection is lacking. This simulation study generated synthetic coating batch trajectories by perturbing a mechanistic spray-coating model with realistic noise distributions estimated from 26 historical production batches of aqueous HPMC-coated tablets at the 30-litre scale. MPCA monitoring models were built from reference sets of varying size (n = 5, 10, 15, 20 batches) and composition (random selection versus diversity-maximised selection using maximum dissimilarity). End-point detection sensitivity and false alarm rate were evaluated over 200 simulated test batches per condition. Models built from diversity-maximised sets of 10–15 batches achieved comparable performance to randomly selected sets of 20 batches (sensitivity 91% vs. 89%, false alarm rate 5.1% vs. 5.4% at 95% confidence). Models built from fewer than eight reference batches showed markedly degraded sensitivity (below 75%). Practical recommendations for reference batch selection in routine coating operations are provided.

title: Evaluating Compression Schemes for Posting Lists in Low-Resource Server Environments
abstract: Posting-list compression directly affects both the memory footprint and decode throughput of full-text search engines. We systematically compare seven integer-compression codecs—including FOR-delta, PForDelta, Simple-8b, and a bitpacking variant—across three corpora of 1 million, 10 million, and 50 million documents sourced from Serbian, Croatian, and Hungarian web crawls. Experiments are conducted on commodity hardware with 16 GB RAM to reflect the constraints typical of small research or company deployments. PForDelta achieves the best decode throughput at 1.1 billion integers per second on the largest corpus, while a tuned FOR-delta variant yields the smallest on-disk footprint at 2.3 bits per integer. We also report how codec choice interacts with query selectivity: high-frequency terms favour block-oriented codecs, whereas rare-term queries are insensitive to codec selection. Practical guidance is provided for operators choosing codecs without exhaustive tuning budgets.

title: A Sharded Query Broker for Sub-100 ms Retrieval over Fifty Index Partitions
abstract: Scaling a search service beyond a single machine introduces coordinator overhead that can dominate end-to-end latency when shard count is large. We design and evaluate a sharded query broker that uses a two-phase scatter–gather protocol with early termination: in the first phase, each shard returns only top-k document identifiers and their scores; in the second phase, only shards holding documents that could affect the global top-k are asked for full postings. Tested on a 50-shard cluster indexing 200 million documents (a synthetic web corpus generated from Common Crawl metadata), the broker keeps 95th-percentile latency below 94 ms for single-term queries and below 140 ms for three-term Boolean conjunctions at 500 queries per second. A comparison with a naïve full-scatter baseline shows a 41% latency reduction with less than 0.1% loss in NDCG@10.
venue: Proceedings of the Symposium on Scalable Data Management Systems (SSDMS)

title: Distributed Full-Text Indexing for Heterogeneous Document Collections: Architectures and Trade-offs
abstract: This book chapter surveys architectures for distributed full-text indexing, focusing on the trade-offs between document-partitioned and term-partitioned layouts when collections are heterogeneous in language, format, and update frequency. We categorise existing systems along four axes: partitioning strategy, merge policy, fault tolerance mechanism, and query routing logic. For each axis we review the academic literature from 2005 to 2016 and relate design choices to measurable outcomes: index freshness, query latency distribution, and hardware utilisation. A recurring finding is that document-partitioned layouts tolerate heterogeneous update rates better, while term-partitioned layouts reduce per-query network traffic for vocabulary-rich corpora. The chapter closes with a discussion of open problems, including the integration of real-time segment merging with batch reindexing and the impact of multilingual tokenisation on partition balance.

title: Incremental HNSW Index Updates Under Concurrent Write Load
abstract: Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs provide high recall and low query latency for approximate nearest-neighbour search but were originally designed for static datasets. We study how concurrent insertions and deletions affect graph connectivity and search quality when updates arrive at rates between 500 and 10,000 vectors per second. Using a 768-dimensional sentence-embedding corpus of 8 million documents (generated with an open encoder trained on multilingual Wikipedia), we measure recall@10 degradation as a function of the fraction of deleted nodes not yet compacted. At 15% uncompacted deletions, recall falls by 3.1 percentage points. We propose a lightweight background compaction scheduler that monitors the deleted-node ratio and triggers partial graph reconstruction during low-traffic windows, recovering recall to within 0.6 points of the static baseline without pausing query serving. Experiments run on a single 40-core server with 256 GB RAM.

title: Hybrid Sparse–Dense Retrieval: Combining BM25 and Vector Indexes Without Score Normalisation Heuristics
abstract: Combining a lexical BM25 index with a dense vector index requires merging scores from incompatible distributions. Most practical systems rely on hand-tuned linear interpolation weights or min–max normalisation, both of which are sensitive to corpus and query distribution shifts. We propose a rank-based fusion approach grounded in reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) that requires no score normalisation and is calibrated using a small set of 500 labelled query–document pairs. Evaluation on two corpora—a 3-million-document Serbian legal archive and a 7-million-document multilingual news collection—shows that the proposed method matches or exceeds the best normalisation baseline on NDCG@10 (gains of 1.8 and 2.4 points respectively) while being robust to out-of-distribution query sets. Latency overhead compared to BM25 alone is 22 ms at the 95th percentile on the larger corpus when vector retrieval runs on GPU.

title: Learned Sparse Retrieval for Low-Resource South Slavic Languages
abstract: Learned sparse retrieval models such as SPLADE expand query and document terms using transformer-derived weights, producing sparse vectors that are indexed in a standard inverted index. Their effectiveness on languages other than English is less studied. We fine-tune a multilingual base transformer on Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian document–query pairs assembled from publicly available court decisions and parliamentary records, producing a total of 280,000 training triples. The resulting model is evaluated on three held-out test sets. MRR@10 improves by 6.1, 4.8, and 5.3 points over BM25 on the Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian sets respectively. Index size is 2.1× that of BM25, and query latency at the 95th percentile is 38 ms on a CPU-only server. We also report the effect of training set size, showing useful gains above approximately 40,000 triples.

title: Tiered Vector Storage: Exploiting NVMe and DRAM Hierarchies for ANN Index Serving
abstract: Dense vector indexes for ANN search are memory-intensive; billion-scale deployments frequently exceed available DRAM. We design a tiered storage manager that partitions HNSW graph layers across DRAM and NVMe, keeping upper graph layers and frequently accessed vectors in DRAM while spilling lower layers to NVMe. Access patterns are tracked with a lightweight frequency counter and a decay factor that deprioritises temporally stale vectors. On a 1.5-billion-vector index (768 dimensions, float16) requiring 2.2 TB uncompressed, the tiered system achieves 89.1% recall@10 using 128 GB DRAM plus 2 TB NVMe, compared to 94.3% recall with full DRAM loading. Query throughput at this recall level is 1,340 queries per second, a 4.2× improvement over a pure NVMe baseline. The implementation builds on an open-source ANN library with a custom I/O scheduler.

title: Distributed Stream Processing: Architectures, Algorithms, and Deployment
abstract: This book chapter surveys the architectural space of distributed stream processing systems, covering foundational data models (data streams, continuous queries, operator graphs), core algorithmic challenges (join algorithms, windowing, state management, fault tolerance), and deployment considerations on both on-premises clusters and cloud-native infrastructure. The chapter is structured in three parts. The first part establishes formal definitions and a taxonomy of processing guarantees (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once). The second part surveys algorithms for the main operator classes—filters, aggregations, joins, and enrichments—with emphasis on complexity trade-offs under varying data distributions. The third part addresses operational concerns: resource allocation, monitoring, schema management, and integration with batch systems. Representative open-source and commercial systems are discussed as illustrative examples without prescriptive endorsement. Annotated references guide readers toward primary literature for each subtopic. The chapter is intended for graduate students and practitioners with prior exposure to database systems and parallel computing.

title: Phenolic characterisation of elderberry accessions from a Serbian field gene bank using LC-MS/MS: identification of minor compounds not detected by HPLC-DAD
abstract: A collection of 18 Sambucus nigra accessions maintained at the Serbian Plant Genetic Resources Centre was re-analysed using LC-MS/MS to complement earlier HPLC-DAD datasets generated between 1997 and 2013. Fourteen previously undetected or tentatively identified compounds were resolved, including three kaempferol glycosides, two quercetin derivatives, and feruloylquinic acid. Chrysanthemin (cyanidin-3-glucoside) remained the dominant anthocyanin across all accessions, but two accessions showed elevated concentrations of pelargonidin-3-glucoside (up to 0.8 mg g−1 DW), a compound not previously reported in Pannonian elderberry material. Total identified phenolic compounds ranged from 28 to 41 per accession. The revised compound list updates the reference chromatographic library held at the Faculty of Agriculture and provides a basis for chemotyping the gene bank collection. The study underscores the value of upgrading analytical platforms when revisiting archived plant material.

title: Flavonoid composition of wild elderberry populations from the Vojvodina lowlands: a baseline survey
abstract: A survey of 14 wild-growing Sambucus nigra populations collected from riparian and field-margin sites across Vojvodina was conducted to establish a baseline flavonoid profile. Berry samples were harvested at full maturity over two consecutive seasons (1995–1996) and extracted with acidified methanol. HPLC-DAD analysis resolved seven major flavonoids, with cyanidin-3-glucoside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside accounting for 78–85% of total anthocyanin content across populations. Total polyphenol content ranged from 412 to 891 mg gallic acid equivalents per 100 g fresh weight, with significant inter-population variability. Rutin concentrations varied from 1.2 to 4.7 mg per g dry weight. The data suggested that edaphic factors—particularly soil organic matter and moisture retention—correlated more strongly with polyphenol accumulation than geographic distance between sites. These findings formed the reference dataset for subsequent stress physiology studies by the group.

title: Rutin accumulation in elderberry leaves and inflorescences as a function of altitude and continentality across a Pannonian–Dinaric transect
abstract: Leaves and fresh inflorescences were collected from 22 Sambucus nigra individuals distributed along an elevational and continentality gradient from 80 m a.s.l. in the Vojvodina plain to 780 m in the Fruška Gora foothills. Rutin was quantified by HPLC after enzymatic hydrolysis and direct injection methods. Rutin content in leaves ranged from 6.3 mg g−1 DW at lowland sites to 14.8 mg g−1 DW at foothill sites, while inflorescence rutin ranged from 3.1 to 9.4 mg g−1 DW. Multiple regression analysis attributed 51% of the variance in rutin to mean summer temperature and 22% to soil pH, with altitude itself explaining relatively little once climate variables were included. The study provides empirical data relevant to the sourcing of elderflower raw material for food and nutraceutical processing in the western Balkans region.

title: Proline and malondialdehyde dynamics in elderberry under progressive drought: links to polyphenol upregulation
abstract: To examine oxidative stress markers alongside polyphenol responses, potted plants of accession SN-PAN-04 were exposed to progressive withholding of irrigation until leaf water potential reached −1.2 MPa, then rewatered. Leaf proline content, malondialdehyde (MDA, as an index of lipid peroxidation), hydrogen peroxide, and total anthocyanin content were measured at five time points. Proline increased sixfold by day 14 of water withholding; MDA rose by 2.3-fold at day 14 but returned to near-baseline 72 hours after rewatering. Total anthocyanin in leaves peaked at day 10 (3.1-fold increase over controls) and remained elevated for five days post-rewatering, suggesting that anthocyanin accumulation precedes peak oxidative damage and may serve a photoprotective rather than purely reactive role. The temporal dissociation between MDA and anthocyanin peaks is discussed in relation to reactive oxygen species signalling.

title: Elderberry as a functional ingredient: agronomic and phytochemical requirements for raw material standardisation in the Pannonian region
abstract: This chapter reviews the agronomic management practices, harvest timing, and post-harvest handling procedures that influence the polyphenol content of Sambucus nigra berries destined for food and nutraceutical processing in the Pannonian Basin. Drawing on a decade of experimental data from the Rimski Šančevi common-garden trial and published literature, threshold values for TPC (≥600 mg GAE per 100 g FW) and TAC (≥6 mg CGE per g FW) are proposed as raw material quality criteria. The chapter addresses how irrigation deficit management (targeting −0.1 to −0.3 MPa) can enhance polyphenol accumulation without reducing commercial yield below economically viable thresholds. Considerations for small-scale growers in Serbia, Hungary, and Romania are included, alongside a brief discussion of traceability and certification schemes applicable to nutraceutical ingredients in the EU regulatory framework.

title: Seasonal dynamics of chlorogenic acid in the bark, leaves, and berries of Pannonian elderberry over the vegetative cycle
abstract: Chlorogenic acid (CGA) content was tracked monthly from budbreak to leaf senescence in bark, leaf lamina, and developing berries of accession SN-PAN-02, chosen for its high CGA titre established in earlier work. Samples were collected from 10 individuals at the Rimski Šančevi orchard across two complete vegetative seasons (2010–2011). HPLC quantification revealed that bark contained the highest CGA concentrations in early spring (up to 18.4 mg g−1 DW) and that levels declined progressively as the season advanced. Leaf CGA peaked in June–July (7.2–9.1 mg g−1 DW) and corresponded to periods of maximum irradiance. Berry CGA at full maturity was comparatively low (1.8–3.2 mg g−1 DW) relative to other tissues. The seasonal profile suggests that bark harvested at budbreak represents the most CGA-rich tissue, a finding relevant to valorisation of pruning waste from commercial plantations.

title: Stomatal conductance and polyphenol responses of elderberry to simulated late-summer drought typical of Vojvodina climate projections
abstract: Climate projections for Vojvodina indicate an increased frequency of late-summer (August–September) dry spells by mid-century. To evaluate elderberry's physiological response to this pattern, a controlled experiment subjected accession SN-PAN-04 plants to a 28-day drought imposed during fruit development, mimicking projected conditions (soil water potential reaching −0.45 MPa on day 28). Stomatal conductance measured by a portable porometer declined by 78% relative to irrigated controls by day 21. Despite severe stomatal closure, berry anthocyanin content increased by 27% and rutin by 19% compared with controls, while berry fresh weight fell by 31%. Harvest index modelling suggested that moderate water deficit imposed during the final 14 days of fruit development would optimise the polyphenol-to-yield trade-off. Results are discussed in the context of adapting irrigation scheduling in commercial elderberry cultivation to anticipated climate change in the region.

title: Comparing polyphenol retention in dried elderberry products prepared by three low-temperature methods: relevance for small-scale producers in Vojvodina
abstract: Berries of accession SN-PAN-04 harvested at full maturity were processed by freeze-drying, hot-air drying at 45 °C, and vacuum drying at 40 °C, then stored for 0, 3, 6, and 12 months at 4 °C and 20 °C. TPC, TAC, rutin, and chlorogenic acid were measured at each time point. Freeze-drying retained 91–94% of TPC immediately after drying, compared with 74–78% for hot-air and 83–86% for vacuum methods. After 12 months at 20 °C, anthocyanin retention dropped to 61% in freeze-dried material, 44% in hot-air dried, and 53% in vacuum-dried product. Storage temperature had a larger effect on anthocyanin stability than drying method. For small-scale producers without freeze-drying access, vacuum drying with refrigerated storage was identified as the most practical compromise. The data provide quantitative benchmarks for quality specifications in producer–processor contracts.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Annotation for Named Entity Recognition: Workflow Design and Annotator Agreement Analysis
abstract: Named entity recognition annotation is iterative by nature: early model outputs guide annotators toward difficult spans, but annotator disagreement can compound over successive rounds if the workflow is not carefully designed. We constructed a workflow in which two annotators independently label each query batch, adjudication is performed by a third expert only when inter-annotator agreement falls below a Cohen's κ threshold of 0.75, and the adjudicated labels feed directly into the next retraining cycle. The corpus covers biomedical text from a Serbian-language clinical discharge summary dataset of 6,400 sentences. Across 12 rounds of 50 sentences each, κ averages 0.81 with adjudication invoked in 4 of 12 rounds. Final NER F1 on a fixed test set reaches 83.4 %, compared with 79.1 % under a single-annotator baseline with the same labelling budget. We discuss how adjudication frequency and annotator fatigue interact and propose a simple fatigue proxy based on session response time.

title: Predictive growth models for Botrytis on soft fruit in the cold chain
abstract: Botrytis cinerea is the primary postharvest pathogen limiting the commercial shelf life of soft fruits during cold-chain distribution. This work presents a suite of predictive growth models calibrated for B. cinerea on raspberry, strawberry, and blueberry substrates across a temperature range of 0–20 °C and relative humidity levels of 85–100%. Square-root (Ratkowsky) and modified Gompertz primary models were fitted to colony diameter and spore germination data collected under isothermal laboratory conditions. Secondary models describing the influence of temperature and water activity on maximum specific growth rate (μmax) and lag phase duration (λ) were subsequently developed and validated. Model performance was assessed using root mean square error (RMSE), bias factor (Bf), and accuracy factor (Af), with Af values below 1.15 indicating satisfactory predictive capacity across all fruit substrates. Dynamic temperature validation trials using step-change and realistic cold-chain temperature profiles confirmed that the models retained predictive reliability under non-isothermal conditions. The resulting model library is intended for integration into cold-chain decision-support software, enabling logistics operators and packers to forecast spoilage risk in real time. Limitations relating to cultivar variability and co-inoculation with yeast species are discussed as priorities for future model refinement.

title: Temperature abuse during transport: a sensor study of fruit exports
abstract: Temperature deviations during postharvest transport — commonly termed temperature abuse — are a leading driver of premature spoilage and economic loss in the fresh fruit export sector. This study employed a network of miniaturized wireless temperature and relative humidity data loggers deployed across 18 commercial refrigerated truck consignments of Serbian berries (raspberry, blueberry, strawberry) destined for markets in Germany, Austria, and Slovenia. Sensor placement covered pallet core, pallet surface, and truck door-proximal positions to capture spatial heterogeneity. Results revealed that door-proximal positions experienced mean temperature elevations of 3.8 °C above target during loading and unloading events, with cumulative abuse time averaging 4.2 hours per journey. Principal component analysis of sensor profiles identified loading sequence and pre-cooling status as the two strongest predictors of abuse severity. Correlation analysis linked abuse incidents with elevated Botrytis incidence and firmness loss quantified at destination. The study provides a field-validated evidence base for the adoption of stricter pre-cooling protocols and improved door-management procedures, and introduces a temperature abuse index (TAI) metric applicable to cold-chain audit frameworks. Recommendations for future sensor infrastructure investment by exporters are presented.

title: Active packaging with natural antimicrobial sachets for blueberry shelf-life extension
abstract: Active packaging systems incorporating volatile antimicrobial agents derived from plant extracts represent a promising complement to conventional modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) for fresh blueberries. This study assessed the efficacy of sachets containing encapsulated thymol and carvacrol — sourced from wild thyme and oregano — integrated into clamshell packaging under a 5% O₂/15% CO₂ atmosphere at 2 °C. Blueberry quality was monitored over 18 days for firmness, total anthocyanin content, weight loss, and microbiological load (total aerobic count and Botrytis incidence). Active MAP sachets reduced total aerobic counts by 1.8 log CFU/g relative to passive MAP controls at day 12 and delayed visible mold onset by four days. Anthocyanin retention was significantly higher in active MAP treatments (p < 0.05), suggesting a secondary antioxidant protective effect. Consumer acceptability scores obtained through a 40-member sensory panel confirmed marketable quality at day 14 for saline-active MAP versus day 10 for passive MAP controls. Migration testing confirmed that thymol and carvacrol residues in fruit tissue remained below European regulatory thresholds. This work demonstrates the practical feasibility of combining MAP gas composition with natural antimicrobial active elements for export-grade blueberry packaging.

title: Integrating predictive microbiology into cold-chain digital twins for berry logistics
abstract: Digital twin frameworks — virtual replicas of physical supply chains updated by real-time sensor data — offer a new paradigm for proactive spoilage management in perishable food logistics. This paper describes the integration of validated predictive microbial growth models for Botrytis cinerea and total aerobic bacteria into a digital twin architecture developed for Serbian berry cold-chain operations. The system ingests temperature and relative humidity streams from IoT sensors placed within refrigerated transport units and storage rooms, feeding real-time inputs into a model library calibrated for raspberry, blueberry, and strawberry substrates. A graphical dashboard presents logistics managers with dynamically updated remaining shelf-life estimates and spoilage risk scores for each consignment. A 12-month pilot deployment covering four exporting companies and 240 consignments demonstrated that digital twin alerts correctly flagged 88% of consignments subsequently confirmed to exhibit elevated spoilage at destination. False-positive rates were 9%, attributed primarily to anomalous sensor placement near evaporator coils. Integration with enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems for automated re-routing decisions is discussed as a near-term development pathway. The study establishes a reproducible blueprint for deploying predictive microbiology within commercial cold-chain digital twin platforms in the Serbian fruit export sector.

title: Effect of pre-cooling rate on modified atmosphere equilibration and raspberry quality
abstract: Rapid and uniform pre-cooling of freshly harvested raspberries prior to MAP sealing is critical for establishing the target equilibrium atmosphere within packaging. This experimental study examined three pre-cooling protocols — forced-air cooling at 2 m/s, hydrocooling at 1 °C, and room cooling as control — applied to raspberry punnets subsequently sealed under a 5% O₂/15% CO₂ MAP at 2 °C storage. Headspace gas composition was monitored at 0, 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours post-sealing using an inline gas analyzer. Fruit core temperature profiles, firmness, respiration rate (CO₂ evolution), and drip loss were recorded throughout a 10-day storage trial. Forced-air cooling achieved target core temperature in 38 minutes compared to 210 minutes for room cooling, and resulted in target headspace O₂ equilibration 14 hours earlier than the room-cooled control. Faster equilibration was associated with significantly lower Botrytis incidence (p < 0.01) and superior firmness retention at day 8. Hydrocooling achieved comparable equilibration speed but introduced elevated free moisture that promoted calyx decay. The findings quantify the shelf-life benefit of investing in forced-air cooling infrastructure and inform revised pre-cooling standard operating procedures for export packers.

title: Shelf-life prediction for strawberries under fluctuating cold-chain temperatures using a stochastic modelling approach
abstract: Deterministic predictive models assume fixed temperature inputs, which rarely reflect the stochastic nature of real-world cold-chain environments. This study presents a stochastic modelling framework for predicting the remaining shelf life of fresh strawberries under realistic fluctuating temperature conditions. A Monte Carlo simulation approach was applied to propagate uncertainty in temperature distribution parameters — derived from 180 sensor-monitored consignments — through a validated secondary model for total aerobic count growth on strawberry. Output distributions of predicted shelf life were compared against observed microbiological end-point data from the same consignments. The stochastic model significantly outperformed its deterministic equivalent in capturing the spread of observed outcomes, with prediction intervals covering 91% of empirical data points. Sensitivity analysis identified mean transport temperature and frequency of door-opening events as the two variables contributing most to shelf-life variance. A simplified probabilistic shelf-life index (PSI) was derived for use by quality managers without specialist modelling expertise. The framework is applicable to other soft fruits and other pathogen or spoilage organism combinations, provided primary growth data are available. This work advances the practical deployment of quantitative risk-informed decision-making in Serbian berry export supply chains.

title: Packaging material permeability screening for MAP of mixed-berry trays
abstract: Mixed-berry trays combining raspberry, blueberry, and blackberry are commercially attractive but present packaging engineering challenges because each species has a distinct optimal modified atmosphere range and a different respiration rate at equivalent temperatures. This study evaluated 12 commercially available polymeric packaging films differing in oxygen transmission rate (OTR) and carbon dioxide transmission rate (CO₂TR) for their suitability in MAP of mixed-berry trays stored at 2 °C. Headspace equilibrium gas compositions were measured at 24-hour intervals over eight days and compared against species-specific target ranges determined from prior single-species trials. Microbiological and firmness data were collected at four-day intervals. A film with OTR of 3,800 cm³/m²/day and CO₂TR of 18,000 cm³/m²/day delivered headspace conditions within acceptable ranges for all three species simultaneously and reduced mold incidence by 55% relative to a standard polyethylene control. Finite element modelling of gas permeation through the film was used to confirm experimental headspace trends and to predict equilibrium under alternative tray fill-weight scenarios. The results provide film specification guidance for packers handling mixed-berry formats and demonstrate that a single film solution can satisfy the conflicting atmosphere requirements of co-packaged fruit species.

title: Food preservation engineering for horticultural products: packaging and cold-chain perspectives
abstract: This book chapter provides a comprehensive treatment of the engineering principles underpinning postharvest preservation of fresh horticultural products, with emphasis on modified atmosphere packaging and cold-chain management. The chapter opens with a review of the biochemical and microbiological deterioration mechanisms that govern shelf life in soft fruits, including ethylene-mediated ripening, oxidative browning, and fungal pathogen proliferation. It then develops the engineering framework for MAP system design, covering gas mass balance modelling, film permeability selection, and tray geometry effects on headspace equilibration dynamics. Cold-chain management is addressed through the lens of predictive microbiology, explaining how primary and secondary models can be linked to temperature monitoring data to generate real-time shelf-life estimates. A section on supply chain integration discusses how MAP and predictive modelling tools can be embedded in digital logistics systems. Case studies drawn from Serbian berry export operations illustrate the translation of laboratory models into operational practice, including a worked example of a forced-air pre-cooling and MAP line for a mid-sized raspberry exporter. The chapter concludes with a forward-looking discussion of emerging active packaging technologies and AI-assisted cold-chain optimisation. It is intended for graduate students and food industry engineers seeking a practically oriented reference.

title: Sensor-based remaining shelf-life labelling for berry exports: a feasibility study
abstract: Static best-before labelling does not reflect the actual quality state of perishable foods subjected to variable cold-chain conditions. This paper reports a feasibility study for implementing sensor-based dynamic remaining shelf-life (RSL) labelling on raspberry and blueberry consignments exported from Serbia. Time-temperature indicator (TTI) labels from two commercial suppliers were benchmarked against data-logger-calibrated predictive model outputs for Botrytis growth and total aerobic count across 24 simulated and 16 real export consignments. TTI colour-response kinetics were characterised at 0, 4, 8, and 12 °C and integrated into an RSL calculation algorithm using an Arrhenius-based temperature dependence model. Agreement between TTI-derived RSL and model-derived RSL was within ±1.2 days for 79% of consignments, which was deemed commercially acceptable by participating exporters. A cost–benefit analysis estimated that TTI-based RSL labelling could reduce consignment rejection rates at destination by 18–24%, yielding a positive return on investment for exporters operating above 50 tonnes per season. Regulatory and labelling compliance considerations under EU food law are discussed, along with the data requirements for formal TTI validation. The study supports the case for piloting RSL labelling in the Serbian berry export sector as part of a broader cold-chain quality assurance programme.

title: Lightweight Anomaly Detection for Resource-Constrained ICS Gateways: A Quantisation and Pruning Study
abstract: Many ICS sites route traffic through ARM-based gateways with 256 MB RAM and single-core processors. This paper evaluates the effect of weight quantisation (32-bit to 8-bit and 4-bit floating point) and structured pruning (removing 10%, 25%, 50% of autoencoder units) on detection performance and inference latency for traffic-based anomaly detectors. Experiments used three autoencoder architectures differing in depth (2, 4, 6 hidden layers) trained on Modbus/TCP and DNP3 captures. 8-bit quantisation reduced model size by 3.7× and inference time by 2.1× with an average AUROC reduction of 0.012. 4-bit quantisation introduced a 0.041 AUROC drop. Structured pruning at 25% improved inference speed by 1.4× with negligible performance loss; at 50%, AUROC declined by 0.028. A combined 8-bit quantised, 25%-pruned model achieved inference at 0.9 ms per 10-second window on an ARM Cortex-A7 target, fitting within a 10 ms cycle budget, making real-time deployment feasible without dedicated hardware accelerators.

title: Statistical Baseline Modelling of Modbus/TCP Traffic in a Substation Automation Network
abstract: This paper describes the construction of per-register statistical baselines for Modbus/TCP traffic captured over six months on a live substation automation testbed. For each register address, empirical distributions of inter-request intervals, payload values, and function code sequences were estimated using kernel density estimation with a Gaussian kernel and bandwidth selected by cross-validation. A one-class detector based on Mahalanobis distance thresholding over a 20-feature vector was evaluated against 14 manually injected attack scenarios, including replay, coil-write injection, and scan sweeps. At a false positive rate of 0.5%, the detector achieved a true positive rate of 91.4% across all attack types. The paper also quantifies the effect of seasonal load variation on baseline drift and proposes a sliding-window recalibration schedule with a 72-hour update period that maintains detection performance without human intervention. Results are compared with a fixed-threshold rule-based baseline, which achieved 67% TPR at the same FPR. The testbed comprised three Siemens-compatible PLCs connected over a deterministic switched Ethernet fabric.

title: One-Class SVM for Detecting Anomalous DNP3 Command Sequences in Water Treatment Control Systems
abstract: One-class support vector machines (OC-SVM) were applied to detect anomalous DNP3 application-layer command sequences in a water treatment SCADA testbed. Feature vectors were constructed from 15-second sliding windows using n-gram frequency histograms of function code and object group pairs, yielding 128-dimensional vectors after principal component analysis retaining 95% of variance. The OC-SVM used an RBF kernel; the nu hyperparameter was swept from 0.01 to 0.20 and selected via leave-one-out cross-validation on a 90-day normal-operation capture (approximately 4.2 million packets). Attack scenarios—unauthorised control block writes, time-sync spoofing, and application-layer flooding—were injected during a separate 14-day test period. The detector achieved an F1 score of 0.87 for unseen attack types not represented during training. Computational overhead was measured at under 3% CPU utilisation on an ARM Cortex-A9 industrial gateway, supporting inline deployment feasibility.

title: Characterising Normal Behaviour in Industrial Ethernet Networks: A Long-Term Measurement Study
abstract: This measurement study presents a 12-month passive capture of traffic from four industrial sites—two discrete manufacturing lines, one water utility, and one district heating plant—totalling approximately 680 GB of raw packet data. The study characterises normal traffic behaviour through 22 statistical descriptors per flow, including coefficient of variation of inter-packet gaps, entropy of destination port distributions, and autocorrelation structure of payload-length time series. Results show that industrial Ethernet traffic exhibits strong periodicity at scales of seconds to hours, with Hurst parameter estimates between 0.61 and 0.79 across sites, indicating long-range dependence. The study documents characteristic differences between Modbus, EtherNet/IP, and proprietary vendor protocols and quantifies seasonal variation. The dataset and feature extraction code are described in sufficient detail to support reproducibility. Findings inform design choices for unsupervised detectors and highlight risks of training on short captures.

title: Isolation Forest Applied to ICS Protocol Traffic: Sensitivity to Contamination Fraction and Window Length
abstract: Isolation Forest was evaluated as a detector for ICS protocol traffic anomalies under controlled variation of two critical hyperparameters: the contamination fraction estimate (ranging from 0.001 to 0.10) and the sliding-window aggregation length (1 s to 300 s). Experiments used a publicly described Modbus/TCP dataset generated on the authors' testbed across five attack classes. Detection rate and false alarm rate were measured at each combination using a 5×2 nested cross-validation design. The contamination fraction had a stronger effect on precision than recall; a mismatch of one order of magnitude reduced average precision from 0.91 to 0.63. Window length affected recall for short-burst attacks more than for persistent anomalies. An empirical calibration procedure based on unlabelled holdout data is proposed and benchmarked. The paper provides a practical guide for practitioners deploying tree-based anomaly detectors in environments where ground-truth labels are unavailable.

title: Autoencoder-Based Reconstruction Error for Anomaly Scoring in PROFINET IO Traffic
abstract: A shallow fully-connected autoencoder with a 48-32-16-32-48 architecture was trained on PROFINET IO cyclic data exchange traffic captured from an automotive body-assembly line. The encoder compressed 48-dimensional per-cycle feature vectors—including cycle time jitter, alarm status byte distributions, and data record checksum statistics—into a 16-dimensional bottleneck. Reconstruction error was used as an anomaly score. The network was trained on 30 days of normal operation (approximately 2.1 million cycles) using stochastic gradient descent with batch size 256. Anomaly scoring was tested against seven fault conditions introduced by a cooperating maintenance team, including sensor dropout, network congestion injection, and controller firmware substitution. The autoencoder achieved an area under the ROC curve of 0.94 across all fault types, compared with 0.81 for a PCA-based reconstruction baseline. Inference latency was 0.4 ms per cycle on a standard x86 edge server, compatible with 10 ms scan cycle requirements.

title: Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control Systems
abstract: This book chapter surveys statistical and machine-learning approaches to anomaly detection in ICS environments, focusing on network-level traffic analysis rather than host-based or physical-process monitoring. The chapter covers the statistical properties of ICS traffic that distinguish it from enterprise IT traffic—determinism, periodicity, limited state space—and how these properties can be exploited by unsupervised methods. Covered algorithms include univariate control charts, multivariate Gaussian models, kernel density estimators, one-class SVMs, Isolation Forest, and autoencoders, with discussion of their assumptions, computational requirements, and suitability for embedded deployment. Protocol-specific considerations are provided for Modbus, DNP3, EtherNet/IP, and PROFINET. The chapter closes with a discussion of evaluation methodology challenges, including the scarcity of labelled datasets, the difficulty of representative attack injection, and the trade-off between false alarm rate and response latency. Representative results from the published literature are tabulated.

title: Evaluating the Effect of Protocol Encryption on Traffic-Based Anomaly Detection: OPC UA Security Mode Comparison
abstract: OPC UA supports three security modes—None, Sign, and SignAndEncrypt—and this paper evaluates how each mode affects the discriminability of traffic features used in unsupervised anomaly detectors. Experiments were conducted on a testbed comprising an OPC UA server, two client applications, and an embedded data historian. Seventeen traffic features extractable from unencrypted traffic were assessed for their availability under Sign and SignAndEncrypt modes using packet capture before and after the application layer. Under SignAndEncrypt, 11 of 17 features became unavailable or uninformative at the packet level; however, timing, packet length distribution, and session-level handshake frequency remained discriminative. A reduced 6-feature one-class SVM trained on these surviving features achieved a detection rate of 0.83 against four attack scenarios, compared with 0.91 for the full 17-feature detector on unencrypted traffic. The paper discusses the implications for passive inline monitoring architectures and proposes a broker-based decryption approach for trusted network segments.

title: A Labelled Packet-Level Dataset of Modbus/TCP Attacks for Evaluating Anomaly Detectors
abstract: This paper describes the collection, annotation, and release of a packet-level Modbus/TCP dataset captured on the ICS testbed at the University of Novi Sad. The dataset spans 21 days of normal operation and 6 days of controlled attack execution, comprising approximately 310 million packets. Eight attack scenarios were implemented: function code scanning, coil mass-write injection, replay with modified values, man-in-the-middle payload substitution, time-synchronisation offset injection, denial-of-service flooding, slow-rate polling exhaustion, and firmware update spoofing. Each packet is labelled with a binary normal/attack flag and a scenario identifier. The paper documents the testbed topology, PLC configuration, traffic generation scripts, and labelling methodology in sufficient detail for reproduction. Baseline results for five detectors—statistical process control, one-class SVM, Isolation Forest, autoencoder, and LSTM-based reconstruction—are reported to enable direct comparison by future researchers. The dataset is hosted on the university repository.

title: Threshold Calibration for ICS Anomaly Detectors Under Imbalanced Operating Conditions
abstract: Anomaly detectors for ICS traffic are typically calibrated by fixing the decision threshold to achieve a target false positive rate estimated on a clean training set. This paper investigates the miscalibration that results when the actual false positive rate at deployment differs from the target, and proposes a post-hoc calibration procedure using a small set of unlabelled operational data. The procedure fits a two-component beta mixture model to the empirical score distribution and uses the mixture weight of the anomalous component as a proxy for the contamination fraction. Experiments on four detectors (OC-SVM, Isolation Forest, autoencoder, and kernel density estimator) across three ICS protocol datasets show that the calibration procedure reduces the gap between nominal and actual FPR from a mean of 3.1 percentage points to 0.4 percentage points. The paper also quantifies sensitivity to the choice of beta mixture initialisation and provides practical recommendations for operators setting alert thresholds.

title: Comparing Score Aggregation Strategies for Multi-Protocol ICS Anomaly Detection
abstract: Industrial sites often run several ICS protocols concurrently; a single anomaly may manifest in traffic from multiple protocols or only one. This paper compares six score aggregation strategies—maximum, mean, product, Dempster-Shafer combination, learned linear combination, and a voting threshold rule—for combining per-protocol anomaly scores from Modbus, DNP3, and EtherNet/IP detectors deployed simultaneously on the same network segment. A testbed with all three protocol stacks was operated for 45 days, and 18 multi-protocol and single-protocol attack scenarios were injected over a 10-day evaluation period. The learned linear combination, trained on a 5-day clean holdout with synthetic contamination, achieved the highest balanced accuracy (0.91) but required labelled data for weight estimation. The Dempster-Shafer rule achieved 0.88 without labelled data. The maximum rule performed consistently below 0.80. Results provide concrete guidance for operators designing multi-sensor detection pipelines.

title: Protocol-Agnostic Anomaly Detection Using Byte-Level Feature Extraction from ICS Application Payloads
abstract: Most ICS anomaly detectors are designed for a specific protocol and rely on parsed field values. This paper investigates a protocol-agnostic approach in which raw application-layer payload bytes from the first 64 bytes of each PDU are used to construct feature vectors via byte-frequency histograms augmented with bigram entropy and mean absolute deviation of byte values. A one-class SVM and an Isolation Forest were trained on mixed-protocol captures from a testbed running Modbus, DNP3, and a proprietary vendor protocol for which no parser was available. The proprietary protocol represented 31% of traffic. Against seven attack scenarios including vendor-protocol-specific command injection, the protocol-agnostic detectors achieved AUROC values of 0.89 and 0.87 respectively, compared with 0.94 for a protocol-aware Modbus detector applied only to Modbus traffic. The paper discusses cases where protocol-agnostic features are sufficient and where parsed fields remain necessary, providing a decision framework for practitioners deploying detectors on heterogeneous industrial networks.

title: Unsupervised anomaly detection on Modbus traffic
abstract: Industrial control systems increasingly rely on Modbus, a legacy serial communication protocol widely deployed in manufacturing and critical infrastructure environments. Despite its prevalence, Modbus lacks built-in security mechanisms, making it highly susceptible to network-based attacks. This paper presents an unsupervised anomaly detection framework specifically designed for Modbus traffic analysis. The proposed approach leverages autoencoder-based neural networks trained exclusively on benign traffic to establish a baseline behavioural profile of legitimate industrial communications. Anomalies are identified by measuring reconstruction error against learned normal patterns, without requiring labelled attack data. The framework is evaluated on a synthetic dataset generated from a real-world programmable logic controller testbed, covering scenarios such as unauthorised function code injection, coil manipulation, and replay attacks. Experimental results demonstrate detection rates exceeding 94% across all attack categories, with a false positive rate below 2%. The paper also analyses the impact of traffic window size and encoding granularity on detection performance, offering practical guidance for deployment in resource-constrained industrial environments.

title: Threat modelling for smart building controllers
abstract: Smart building automation systems increasingly integrate heterogeneous controllers managing heating, ventilation, access control, and fire suppression, all connected over IP-based networks. This convergence introduces significant attack surfaces that are rarely addressed through systematic security engineering. This paper applies a structured threat modelling methodology—adapted from STRIDE and augmented with ICS-specific threat categories—to a representative smart building controller architecture. The analysis identifies seventeen distinct threat scenarios spanning spoofing of sensor inputs, tampering with actuator commands, and denial-of-service against building management gateways. For each threat, the paper proposes corresponding mitigations including cryptographic command authentication, rate-limiting policies, and network segmentation strategies. A comparative evaluation against an unmitigated baseline system is conducted using a simulation environment, demonstrating measurable risk reduction across all identified threat categories. The findings offer actionable security guidance for building automation vendors and facility managers deploying next-generation smart infrastructure.

title: A comparative study of intrusion detection architectures for SCADA networks
abstract: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) networks form the backbone of critical infrastructure sectors including energy distribution, water treatment, and transportation. Protecting these networks from cyber intrusions requires detection systems capable of operating on highly specialised industrial protocols while maintaining low false-positive rates in continuous operation. This paper conducts a systematic comparative evaluation of five intrusion detection architectures—signature-based, specification-based, statistical anomaly, deep learning, and hybrid approaches—applied to a common SCADA testbed. Each architecture is assessed across four attack categories: reconnaissance, command injection, man-in-the-middle, and denial-of-service. Performance is measured in terms of detection accuracy, latency, resource consumption, and adaptability to concept drift. Results show that hybrid architectures combining specification-based rules with neural anomaly scoring achieve the best overall balance, while purely deep-learning-based systems exhibit higher sensitivity to protocol version variability. The paper concludes with a decision framework to guide practitioners in selecting appropriate detection strategies based on operational constraints.

title: Federated learning for distributed intrusion detection across IoT edge nodes
abstract: Internet of Things deployments in industrial and smart city environments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous network traffic across geographically distributed edge nodes. Centralising this data for intrusion detection raises significant privacy and bandwidth concerns, particularly in multi-stakeholder environments. This paper proposes a federated learning framework for distributed intrusion detection, wherein each edge node trains a local anomaly detection model on its own traffic and periodically shares only model gradient updates with a central aggregation server. The aggregated global model is then redistributed to participating nodes, enabling collective knowledge improvement without raw data exposure. The framework is evaluated on a purpose-built IoT testbed consisting of twenty-four heterogeneous edge devices simulating smart metering, environmental sensing, and industrial actuation scenarios. Results demonstrate that the federated approach achieves detection accuracy within 3% of a centralised baseline while reducing data transmission overhead by over 80%. The paper also investigates the robustness of the framework against poisoning attacks introduced by compromised edge nodes.

title: Threat modelling in IIoT supply chains: identifying lateral movement pathways
abstract: Industrial Internet of Things supply chains encompass multiple layers of hardware vendors, firmware providers, system integrators, and end operators, each introducing potential vulnerabilities that adversaries may exploit for lateral movement across organisational boundaries. This paper presents a threat modelling methodology tailored to IIoT supply chain architectures, extending traditional STRIDE analysis with supply-chain-specific threat categories including firmware substitution, third-party library poisoning, and vendor credential reuse. A reference IIoT architecture involving a six-tier supply chain is modelled, and attack graphs are constructed to identify the most probable lateral movement pathways between tiers. Quantitative risk scores are assigned using a modified CVSS-based scoring system adapted for operational technology contexts. The analysis reveals that firmware update channels and remote maintenance interfaces constitute the highest-risk lateral movement vectors. Mitigation recommendations include cryptographic firmware signing, role-based access segmentation across supply chain tiers, and continuous behavioural monitoring of maintenance sessions. The framework is validated through a tabletop exercise with industrial practitioners.

title: Network segmentation strategies for securing legacy OT environments
abstract: Operational technology environments in manufacturing and utility sectors frequently rely on decades-old equipment designed without cybersecurity considerations. Retrofitting strong security controls onto such systems is often impractical, making network segmentation one of the most effective available defences. This paper systematically evaluates five segmentation strategies—air-gapping, DMZ insertion, unidirectional gateways, micro-segmentation using software-defined networking, and VLAN-based isolation—across three representative legacy OT environments modelled after real-world process control architectures. Each strategy is assessed against a standardised threat catalogue derived from known ICS incident reports, covering scenarios such as ransomware propagation, historian server compromise, and remote access exploitation. The evaluation employs a simulation-driven methodology combining network topology modelling with attack path analysis. Results indicate that micro-segmentation combined with unidirectional gateways at critical zone boundaries provides the highest resilience against multi-stage attacks, though at significant configuration complexity. The paper provides a practical scoring matrix to assist security engineers in selecting segmentation approaches based on available resources and operational constraints.

title: Detecting replay attacks on DNP3 protocol in smart grid communications
abstract: DNP3 is a widely deployed communication protocol in smart grid environments, facilitating data exchange between substations, remote terminal units, and control centres. Despite extensions introduced in DNP3 Secure Authentication version 5, many deployments remain vulnerable to replay attacks due to misconfiguration or the use of older protocol variants. This paper presents a lightweight detection mechanism for DNP3 replay attacks based on temporal sequence analysis of application-layer message fields. The proposed detector monitors request-response timing patterns, sequence counter consistency, and message fragment ordering to identify anomalous retransmission behaviour indicative of replay activity. The mechanism is implemented as a passive network probe requiring no modifications to existing field devices. Evaluation on a hardware-in-the-loop smart grid testbed shows that the detector correctly identifies replay attacks with 97.3% precision and 95.8% recall, while maintaining a processing latency below 12 milliseconds per packet—well within operational requirements. The paper further discusses integration of the detector into existing security information and event management pipelines used in utility control centres.

title: Cybersecurity frameworks for critical infrastructure protection: a survey and gap analysis
abstract: Critical infrastructure sectors—including energy, water, transportation, and telecommunications—face an evolving and increasingly sophisticated threat landscape. Numerous cybersecurity frameworks have been developed to guide operators in assessing and improving their security posture, including NIST CSF, IEC 62443, NERC CIP, and ISA/IEC standards. Despite their widespread adoption, significant gaps remain in how these frameworks address emerging challenges such as cloud-connected OT environments, AI-driven attacks, and supply chain interdependencies. This survey systematically reviews twelve major cybersecurity frameworks applicable to critical infrastructure, evaluating them across dimensions of scope, implementation guidance, assessment methodology, and adaptability to ICS-specific threats. A structured gap analysis reveals that most frameworks inadequately address real-time anomaly detection requirements, provide insufficient guidance on IoT integration, and lack concrete metrics for evaluating detection and response effectiveness. The paper proposes a consolidated gap taxonomy and outlines a research agenda addressing the most critical deficiencies. It is intended as a reference for both practitioners implementing security programmes and researchers developing next-generation framework components.

title: Intrusion detection in resource-constrained IoT devices using lightweight recurrent models
abstract: Deploying intrusion detection directly on resource-constrained IoT devices such as microcontroller-based sensors and actuators presents fundamental challenges in terms of memory footprint, computational overhead, and energy consumption. This paper investigates the feasibility of implementing lightweight recurrent neural network models—specifically truncated LSTM and GRU variants—on devices with fewer than 256 KB of RAM. A model compression pipeline is developed that combines quantisation, pruning, and knowledge distillation to reduce model size by up to 94% relative to full-precision baselines, while preserving detection accuracy above 90% across standard IoT attack benchmarks. The compressed models are deployed on three representative IoT platforms and evaluated under realistic workload conditions. Power consumption measurements indicate that continuous on-device inference adds less than 4 mW overhead, making deployment feasible even on battery-powered nodes. The paper also proposes an adaptive inference strategy that dynamically reduces model complexity during high-load periods to prevent resource exhaustion. Results suggest that on-device intrusion detection is practically achievable for a broad class of constrained IoT deployments.
